fullText:
SHANGHAI, Sept 26 (Reuters) - The United States and China have agreed to reduce tariffs on $30 billion of goods and launch a dialogue on AI, both countries said following President Xi ‌Jinping's visit to Washington.

The tariff reductions would apply to US exports such as agricultural goods, wood ‌and cosmetics, as well as US imports including small appliances, toys, decorations, a White House statement said on Friday.

"The two countries reached ​consensus on recommendations for more favorable tariff treatment for $30 billion of non-sensitive goods in each direction," the White House said.

The three-day summit between Xi and President Donald Trump, which ended on Friday, showcased personal diplomacy rather than big public breakthroughs. Xi has since landed in Beijing, Chinese state news agency Xinhua reported on Saturday.

The two sides ‌also agreed to set up a trade ⁠council and extend the outcomes of earlier talks in Kuala Lumpur, the Chinese Foreign Ministry said.

The agreement follows a move by the world's two largest economies to extend by ⁠two months a trade truce that had been due to expire on November 10, allowing more time to work on a potentially bigger trade deal, US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday.

"This historic visit enriched the constructive ​and stable ​China-US relationship, upheld the overall stability of bilateral ties, ​opened a new chapter in China-US relations, and ‌will have a far-reaching impact on world peace and development," Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi said in a statement.

On artificial intelligence, the two sides agreed to hold a dialogue on the technology's risks and benefits, with the next round of discussions set for November, and to set up a communication channel for AI-related incidents, the Chinese Foreign Ministry and the White House said.

The White House said that the leaders had agreed ‌to use the term "super intelligence" in place of "artificial intelligence."

In a ​separate statement, the Chinese ministry said that Beijing valued Washington's use ​of the new term.

As AI technology continues ​to advance, the two sides should step up exchanges and work toward consensus in ‌line with new developments, it said.

The two sides ​also agreed to support each ​other in hosting the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation leaders' meeting and the Group of 20 summit, with both leaders planning to attend the gatherings hosted by the other.

On foreign policy, the leaders agreed ​that Iran should fulfil its commitment not ‌to develop nuclear weapons, and that no country or entity should impose transit tolls on ​international waterways, both countries said.

title: House Democrats plan vast oversight of Trump admin. Impeachment is an option.
description:
— House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda, with investigations of President Donald Trump, his family and his administration if the party sweeps control of the chamber from Republicans in the November elections.
The undertaking is as robust as it is daunting, spanning several House committees. With majority power comes bigger budgets and staff, and the ability to investigate, subpoena and potentially course-correct what the Democrats say are widespread corruption and abuses of power. Impeachment of the Republican president and Cabinet officials is not off the table.
“There is a cost to the American people of the out-of-control corruption,” said Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker if Democrats win control at the Capitol.
fullText:
WASHINGTON (AP) — House Democrats are preparing a vast oversight agenda, with investigations of President Donald Trump, his family and his administration if the party sweeps control of the chamber from Republicans in the November elections.

The undertaking is as robust as it is daunting, spanning several House committees. With majority power comes bigger budgets and staff, and the ability to investigate, subpoena and potentially course-correct what the Democrats say are widespread corruption and abuses of power. Impeachment of the Republican president and Cabinet officials is not off the table.

"There is a cost to the American people of the out-of-control corruption," said Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York, who is in line to become House speaker if Democrats win control at the Capitol.

"If folks have been stealing from the American people, shortchanging the American people or screwing over the American people," Jeffries said, "we are going to hold the crooks accountable."

Congress has enormous ability to conduct oversight of the executive branch as part of its power as a coequal branch of government, and a road map for the Democratic-run investigations has already been set by the almost daily letters lawmakers send to the administration and in amicus court filings.

Democrats are asking about the money-making by Trump and his family, whose wealth has grown dramatically since he returned to the White House in January 2025. They are investigating the potential civil rights violations of Americans killed protesting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations and of detained immigrants being deported to faraway countries. They have fought the closing of the Kennedy Center, launched investigations into private funding of the America at 250 celebrations and tracked the shuttering of federal operations, including the U.S. Agency for International Development.

New questions emerge daily, including the Trump family's recent acknowledgment that a weekend wedding party for the president's son Donald Trump Jr. was partly funded by a Russian oligarch, with reportedly close ties to the Kremlin.

Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md., who is in line to become the chairman of the Judiciary Committee, characterized the issues involved as "gargantuan."

"We need to zero in quickly on the forms of systemic corruption that have cost the public huge amounts of money," Raskin told The Associated Press, "and where there are legislative cures available."

Jeffries will almost certainly be under pressure from the far left to move more swiftly to articles of impeachment against Trump, who during his first became the first president to be twice impeached by the House. Both times, he was acquitted by the Senate.

Impeaching the president a third time may not hold the currency that it once did. Democrats will more likely focus their impeachment efforts on Cabinet members. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth already faces articles of impeachment from a Republican, Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, over his leadership at the Pentagon and his management of the Iran war.

"We haven't ruled anything out," Jeffries said recently about the tools available to Congress, "and we haven't ruled anything in."

The White House is likely to play hardball if confronted with investigations, and Democrats are bracing for an administration that potentially ignores subpoenas or refuses to turn over paperwork that lawmakers are demanding.

The Democrats are also reaching beyond the administration into various corporate and business entities for potential wrongdoing.

Ranking Democratic lawmakers who are in line to lead committees if power shifts are beginning to chart the investigations they plan to tackle.

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the top Democrat now on the Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has outlined five priorities, including Trump family business dealings, the administration's handling of the Jeffrey Epstein investigation and ICE operations.

"We're already doing work," Garcia told the AP.

He also mentioned the Department of Health and Human Services under Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., as well as broader allegations of corporate corruption.

The top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee, Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York, whose jurisdiction includes the State Department, said the committee plans to investigate Trump's international dealings, including around the Iran war.

He expects the committee will also look into the administration's Venezuela operations — from the military strikes on alleged drug boats in the Caribbean and Pacific waters to the U.S. partnership with a private company to develop and access the South American country's oil.

Rep. Jared Huffman of California, the ranking Democrat at the Natural Resources Committee, which overseas the Interior Department and its National Park Service operations, has begun digging into Trump's "vanity projects," including the demolition of the White House's East wing for a new ballroom and the president's proposed arch.

Huffman and other committee members have also been eyeing the Trump family's role in various minerals deals.

At the committee's last session before lawmakers recessed to campaign for the midterm elections, Huffman said that if Democrats take charge, he plans to call witnesses, put them under oath and follow the evidence where it leads.

"When people ask what will we do," he said he responds, "My answer is simple. We'll use those tools. We'll act like the Congress."

title: Pope Leo praises young people as 700,000 gather for open-air Mass in Paris
description: Watch: Huge crowds greeted the Pope as he travelled down the...
fullText:
Pope Leo XIV has praised the "enthusiasm, energy and commitment" young people bring to the Catholic Church as dense crowds attended an open-air Mass in Paris.

An estimated 700,000 people had gathered for the Mass celebrated by the Pope from a special altar on the Place de la Concorde, on the second day of his four-day visit to France.

It began after the pontiff rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue waving to crowds from his open-topped popemobile.

Many senior politicians attended the Mass. On Friday, the Pope met French President Emmanuel Macron.

During Saturday's Mass, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed".

The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech, describing them as "today's Church".

"How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said.

After being welcomed by Macron on Friday, the Pope was joined by 80,000 young people at the Stade de France in northern Paris.

Macron did not attend Saturday's event and will not be at any of the Pope's Masses during his visit, largely to avoid appearing to breach France's strict rules on the separation of Church and state.

But the Mass was attended by Macron's wife Brigitte and French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu.

Several candidates for next year's presidential election also attended.

Marine Le Pen of the hard-right National Rally party and conservative Bruno Retailleau were both pictured at the Place de la Concorde ahead of the event, while centrists Édouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal were also spotted.

Earlier on Saturday, the Pope met migrants and volunteers as he visited the Maison Bakhita centre, an association supporting refugees, and praised the organisation for inviting "us to see those who are invisible".

He also stressed the "fundamental role of women in building a civilisation of love".

The Pope issued a warning about the dangers of artificial intelligence (AI) at the start of his visit to France on Friday.

Leo cautioned against "losing our humanity amid a paradise of machines" in wide-ranging remarks to Church and state officials at the Élysée Palace.

Large crowds are expected throughout the remainder of the pontiff's trip, which the Church believes reflects a growing spirituality among the French and other Europeans.

Late on Saturday the Pope flew to south-western town of Lourdes. He prayed at its famous sanctuary, where he will celebrate a Mass on Sunday which 150,000 people have signed up to attend.

The Pope will be in the north-eastern city of Metz on Monday to pay tribute to Robert Schuman (1886-1963), a founding father of the European Union and a fervent Catholic who is a candidate for beatification - a formal recognition that a person is believed to have entered heaven.

Born in Chicago in 1955, Pope Leo XIV was originally called Robert Prevost – a French name.

His paternal grandmother was born in Le Havre in Normandy in 1894. When she married in the US many years later, she and her Italian husband took the name Prevost, which had been her mother's maiden name.

fullText:
James Talarico’s poll lead over Ken Paxton in the crunch Texas Senate battle has fallen by one point according to two new opinion polls, which also showed the number of undecided Texan voters has been reduced.

Democrats are hoping to win control of the Senate at the November midterms and victory in Texas—a traditional Republican stronghold that last elected a Democratic senator in 1988—would significantly boost their chances.

Friday saw the publication of the latest Texas Public Opinion Research survey which polled 1,007 likely Texan voters between September 19 and 22. The poll, which had a 3.6 percent margin of error, found state Representative Talarico leading current Texas Attorney General Paxton by five points with 49 percent of the vote against 44 percent.

The last Texas Public Opinion Research survey, of 1,000 likely Texas voters conducted from August 21-24, gave Talarico a six-point lead, with 48 percent of the vote against Paxton’s 42 percent.

Notably the proportion of undecided voters has also fallen from seven percent in August to three percent this month, with Libertarian candidate Ted Brown also gaining two percentage points. However, the decrease in Talarico’s support remains within the margin of error.

Separately a new Texas Southern University survey gave Talarico a lead of just one point, with 47 percent of the vote against 46 percent for Paxton and three percent for Brown. This survey of 1,800 Texan likely voters took place between September 15 and 19 and has a 2.31 percent margin of error.

Newsweek contacted the Talarico and Paxton senate campaigns for comment via email on Saturday outside of regular office hours.

Talarico leads Paxton according to eight different pollsters, though several are within the margin of error, and thus too close to call.

An Emerson College survey, conducted September 12-14, gave Talarico a 1-point lead with 47 percent of the vote to Paxton's 46 percent. The poll surveyed 1,000 voters with a margin of error of 3 percentage points.

Between August 30 and September 1, AARP surveyed 895 likely voters, giving Talarico a 4-point lead with a 3.3-point margin of error. Similarly, a YouGov/Univision poll of 1,000 registered voters that took place between August 27 and September 4 put Talarico ahead by 5 points, with a 3.6-point margin of error.

He accused Paxton of “dodging debates all year” continuing: “So let’s go to Ken Paxton’s safe space. Let’s do Bret Baier on Fox News. I’ll go into the lions den.”

According to Federal Election Commission (FEC) figures up to June 30 the official Talarico senate campaign raised $31,853,507, significantly ahead of the Paxton campaign on $9,147,100.

The FED data showed 45 percent of donations to Talarico’s campaign came from out of state, with California being the biggest contributor, compared with 17.1 percent for Paxton.

Contact Newsweek editor on this story: Edward Pearcey.

title: ‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness

fullText:
The tech giant has launched a cute ‘little guy’ that can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop

After the recent backlash against Meta’s so-called “pervert” smart glasses, this week Mark Zuckerberg launched a much cuter alternative: the Muse “charm” device.

With a screen that shows a cutesy little avatar, it has drawn comparisons with Tamagotchis. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” the Meta founder told the San Francisco audience.

The “little guy” could fit, like a Labubu, on to a keychain or bag. But unlike a Labubu, the interactive AI assistant will have significant capabilities, including the ability to have live conversations. It can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop.

According to Katie Seaborn, a Cambridge associate professor who has been researching cuteness – creating the science of cute voices within the context of computing – it’s cute because it “basically looks like a baby”.

For Joshua Paul Dale, professor at Chuo University in Tokyo and author of Irresistible: How Cuteness Wired our Brains and Conquered the World: “It’s really significant that along with the wearable charm, Meta also introduced a new pair of smart glasses with no camera. Everyone hates cameras in smart glasses. But if the camera is contained in a charm you wear around your neck, it shifts the agency. Suddenly, you’re not recording people. It’s just a cute little animated avatar looking out on the world.”

An individualised, customisable, and in this case adorable, AI companion, it tracks with Zuckerberg’s commitment to the idea of personal, wearable super-intelligence that you can chat to. As well as a broader shift towards cute technology, cited by forecasters WGSN as a top trend for 2026.

“Clearly,” says Dale, “what Meta is trying to do is make Muse into a companion. And it’s doing it in the simplest possible way … It’s using a very simplified, tiny 2-inch screen to encourage you to anthropomorphise the figure on it so that you treat it as if it’s human even though you know it’s not.”

Its cuteness is, according to Seaborn, “strategic”. “It’s very natural to emerge from this controversy with a technology that uses cuteness because … it’s so weak. Don’t worry about it. You can trust us.”

To try to harness the power of cuteness, according to Seaborn, “makes sense, especially from a big tech perspective because maybe people are getting wise to the ways of current strategies when it comes to people’s attention, their personal data and what have you. And now they’re trying new things that may or may not work”.

Seaborn, who has just moved to the University of Cambridge from Japan, points out that “this is something that is very normal in Japan. So the first thing you notice when you go there is that every single thing has a mascot. The government organisations, the media companies, the businesses, they all have a cute mascot”.

Seaborn has studied the “impacts cuteness can have on people”. “We’ve been seeing cuteness applied as a design strategy for different purposes. We know [that it] has certain impacts on people.” For one thing “cuteness is a way for certain social interactions to take place or to be smoothed over”.

There is also a “natural link between cuteness and deception … I call it ‘charming and disarming’, because one of the things cuteness does to us unconsciously, it’s just how our brain processes it, is lets down our guard. We can’t really help it.”

Whether Muse will catch on when it is released in December, or whether such a blatant attempt to gain trust via an on-screen avatar with cheeks you want to squish will land, remains to be seen. But different generations are likely to react differently. “That’s so AI!” is the phrase gen Alpha are using to dismiss anything they think is inauthentic.

For many gen Zers who are au fait with having a cuddly toy hanging from their bags, most typically in the form of a Labubu, it might feel less of a wrench. For older generations there will be nostalgic associations given its resemblance to older technologies. Embedded in it, says Seaborn, “[is] this legacy of these cute kind of gamified pet sort of things like Tamagotchi and Pocky Pikachu”.

Plus different cultural contexts will affect how it is received. Seaborn’s research has found that “Americans were actually less likely to be deceived compared with Japanese people … Because in Japan robots are heroes, they’re like babies”. Whereas “in western culture they’re often presented in the public imagination as kind of scary, potentially broken, sinister devices”. In UK focus groups, people reported a “gut feeling” that something was wrong when cuteness was part of a deceptive design idea. “People felt like something was off, but they couldn’t articulate what it was.”

But the picture, says Seaborn, is changing. “Because cuteness [or kawaii] has been a cultural export of Japan and other nations for a while now … there might be a slow cultural shift happening in terms of how we orient ourselves towards cuteness and what we accept as adults.”

While Dale is “not rushing out to buy one”, he “will say, however, that when I’m 80 years old I’ll definitely want one of these things. I want to wear it around my neck always, and I want the camera on all the time, so it can tell me where I left my glasses.”

Russell faultless and Hadjar excellent on return - driver ratings
description: BBC Radio 5 Live F1 commentator Harry Benjamin rates how the drivers performed during the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.
fullText:
George Russell led from start to finish as he dominated the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

The victory reduced the championship lead of his Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli to 66 points - from 81 - after the Italian finished fifth, although he had recovered from starting 16th on the grid.

Max Verstappen pushed Russell for the win as he took second place, less than two tenths of a second behind. Fellow Red Bull driver Isack Hadjar completed the podium by finishing third on his return to racing following a wrist injury.

Here are my ratings for how the drivers performed across the whole weekend in Baku.

Pretty difficult to find fault with this one. Fastest on Thursday, produced a stunning qualifying lap to take pole by more than eight tenths and controlled the race before holding off Max Verstappen under huge pressure at the end.

His eighth place in qualifying looked poor on paper but came with genuine power and energy deployment problems. Charged through the field on Saturday, passed Oscar Piastri for second and pushed Russell all the way to the line. An excellent recovery.

What a way to return after three races on the sidelines. Out-qualified Verstappen with fourth on the grid, showed excellent pace early in the race and finished on the podium while also playing the team game when Verstappen came through.

Second on the grid was an excellent qualifying result, although a tow certainly helped him get there. Ferrari simply didn't have the race pace to stay with Russell and the Red Bulls and fourth felt about the maximum available by the end.

A weekend of two very different halves. Crashing out in Q1 was a costly and unnecessary mistake, but he responded with a patient recovery from 16th to fifth despite picking up floor damage during the race.

His qualifying result was hurt by Ferrari's run plan leaving him without the tow he needed, but sixth in both qualifying and the race still made for a fairly quiet weekend. Solid enough, although Leclerc had the upper hand when it mattered.

Recovered again impressively after crashing in practice and starting 15th. Took advantage of the chaos when it came and then stole seventh from Esteban Ocon by the tiniest of margins at the finish. Goes a long way to limiting the grief he might get from punting into his Racing Bulls team-mate at Turn One.

A really strong race from the Haas driver after starting outside the top 10. Made some decisive moves as others fell into trouble and briefly looked set for seventh before Lindblad pinched it on the line.

Good enough to narrowly miss Q3 and stayed in the points despite losing out to Ocon during the race. Contact with Antonelli at the first restart was a slightly messy moment in an otherwise useful result for Haas.

The pace was encouraging and ninth in qualifying would have been Williams' best grid position of the season but failing to slow sufficiently for yellow flags earned him a five-place grid penalty. Recovered from as low as 19th in the race to grab the final point.

Russell wins despite late Verstappen challenge

Norris says Colapinto should be banned after accident

Audi's big upgrade didn't translate into qualifying. However, Hulk recovered reasonably well to 11th thanks to the carnage ahead but lost the final point to Sainz late on.

Back at Racing Bulls after three races with Red Bull and showed reasonable pace to qualify 12th before penalties moved him up the grid. His race was badly affected when team-mate Lindblad made contact with him in the chaotic second restart, leaving 12th a difficult result to judge too harshly.

For most of the weekend this was heading towards a very high score for the McLaren driver. Third in qualifying and running in the podium positions for much of the race. But his big lock-up at Turn One dropped him all the way down the order and threw away a potentially excellent result.

Looked rapid compared with Cadillac team-mate Valtteri Bottas in the early part of the weekend. But a suspected Q2 challenge didn't quite materialise.

Another difficult weekend for Audi despite all the new parts on the car. Out in Q1 alongside Hulkenberg and although he made progress on race day, it was not the return he would have hoped for.

His final qualifying lap was deleted for being set under double-waved yellow flags, leaving him at the back of the order. Almost made it to the finish but found the barriers late on.

The weekend had actually been going well after reaching Q3 and starting ninth. But his enormous lock-up at the second restart wiped out team-mate Pierre Gasly and Lando Norris as well as his own race, turning a potential double points finish for Alpine into nothing.

A really good weekend that deserved so much better. Qualified seventh and was still running there at the final restart before being taken out by his team-mate through no fault of his own.

Not the cleanest weekend for McLaren's world champion. A mistake on his final qualifying lap left him fifth and another lock-up during the race had already cost him places before he became an innocent victim of Colapinto's restart crash.

Was behind Sainz in qualifying before his team-mate's penalty shuffled the grid. His race ended with an error into the barriers at Turn Four which brought out the first safety car, so a difficult weekend despite signs of improvement from the car.

Another weekend where there wasn't much opportunity to show anything. Qualified 19th, took a back-of-grid power-unit penalty and then retired with a mechanical problem in a miserable race for Aston Martin.

Qualified behind Alonso before also taking his own penalty. Another mechanical retirement meant Aston Martin left Baku without either car reaching the finish.

title: Bellamy eyes more history against wounded Denmark
description: Craig Bellamy reflects on his memorable moments against Denmark as his Wales side bid to topple the Danes in the Nations League on Sunday (17:00 BST).
fullText:
When it comes to Wales needing a result, Craig Bellamy and Denmark have been something of a surprise dream fit.

On the back of a 1-0 loss to Portugal in Lisbon, the head coach is straight back down to business as he prepares his side to face the Danes in Copenhagen on Sunday (17:00 BST).

With no wins in their five matches in 2026, Bellamy and Wales sorely need a positive result - particularly as they bid to upset the odds and preserve their Nations League A status.

But Bellamy has an impressive history with Denmark, and the aim is now to create even more.

Do Wales have what it takes to survive League A?

'Workhorse' Koumas growing with Wales

In 1998, Bellamy came off the bench to net an 87th-minute winner - his first competitive international goal - as Wales came from behind to stun Denmark in Euro 2000 qualifying.

It ended Wales' seven-game winless run in competitive matches, and former striker Iwan Roberts - who was an unused substitute in the game - felt the result rescued boss Bobby Gould.

"It was a magnificent header and probably saved Gould," Roberts told the BBC's Feast of Football podcast.

Gould himself said at the time: "All I saw was 14 fantastic Welshmen out there giving everything."

He added: "When Craig scored the winner we were all sitting on the bench blowing it over the line."

Bellamy's own recollection of matters is somewhat different, with some members of the squad perhaps disappointed Gould had been handed a shock lifeline.

"I got loads of stick for it after the game as well, from the players in the changing room, and they weren't too happy," added the Wales boss.

"For me it was one of the happiest moments of my career at 19 years of age, and the players looked at me with such disgust."

Of the game itself, Bellamy said: "The kit was awful; I looked awful.

"I was a young kid coming through at the time, scoring a lot of goals in the Championship. I was 19; everything was going in at that moment.

"The actual reflection of the game, they battered us. To come on, and it was the furthest thought from my mind that I was going to get a winner. It was crazy."

Jay Dasilva - who was born just six months before Bellamy's moment of magic in Copenhagen - revealed the head coach had not mentioned his goal to the squad.

But the Coventry City left-back duly vowed to "pull him up on it" after facing the media on the eve of the Nations League contest with the Danes.

Sunday, 27 September, 17:00 BST

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

A decade later, Bellamy inflicted maximum damage on Denmark once again.

Approximately 15 miles southwest of Parken Stadium, Wales took on Denmark in November 2008, a game in which Aaron Ramsey made his senior international debut.

Bellamy drilled beyond goalkeeper Thomas Sorensen from around 20 yards out in the 77th minute to earn John Toshack's side a surprise friendly victory.

"I asked him to play deeper and go behind, and he still got his chances in the first half and scored the winning goal as well," boss Toshack said after the contest.

Now leading Wales from the sidelines rather than on the pitch, Bellamy has the tough task of toppling Denmark as a coach.

Like Wales, Brian Riemer's side lost their opening Nations League A game on Thursday night as they were beaten 3-2 by Norway in Oslo.

Denmark also failed to qualify for this year's World Cup, as did Bellamy's men, after suffering penalty shootout heartache in the play-offs against Czechia.

With Wales winless since beating North Macedonia in November last year and Denmark without a victory since overcoming the same opponents in the World Cup play-off semi-finals in March, both sides are bidding to end long waits to register a tick in the win column.

Denmark boss Riemer said the fixture with Wales is a "must-win", with Bellamy going on to add that he could "understand the frustrations" of the Danish supporters.

The Wales head coach felt it was wise not to "poke the bear" when it comes to making any predictions about the contest with the somewhat wounded Danes.

But he will be quietly confident that his side have a chance of creating yet more positive headlines against Denmark as they bid to prove they have what it takes to do the business in the top tier of the Nations League.

title: Bristol start with steely victory at Sale
description: Bristol Bears claim a notable win away against Sale Sharks, running in five tries in a 34-24 success at CorpAcq Stadium.
fullText:
Tries: Cowan-Dickie, O'Flaherty 2 Cons: Ford 3 Pen: Ford

Tries: Rees-Zammit 2, Randall 2, Gwilliam Cons: Williams 3 Pen: Williams

Bristol Bears got their Prem campaign off to a fine start as they claimed a bonus-point triumph away to Sale Sharks.

With no newcomers in their starting line-up, Bristol showed the benefit of continuity as they ran in five tries to get up and running in style.

Wales star Louis Rees-Zammit got two of them, Harry Randall matched that with scores either side of half-time, before a 73rd-minute effort from replacement hooker Tomas Gwilliam made certain of victory.

But it was a disappointing first night for the Sharks, who lost no fewer than 13 Prem games last season.

Luke Cowan-Dickie's try had put them ahead early on and Tom O'Flaherty scored two in the second half but they finished short of either of the bonus point markers.

Few Prem sides probably have as much to prove this season as Sale after their run of three successive play-off finishes was emphatically ended by a disappointing seventh place, and they also had a losing home record at CorpAcq Stadium.

They have brought back big names Courtney Lawes and Joe Marchant from France to add more substance as they bid to get back into top-four contention, but this was not a good way to start for Alex Sanderson's team.

The Bears were only one place, but 18 points, above their opponents in the final table in June although their last campaign was undermined by a raft of injuries.

That curse is already strong again this term with new signing from Bath, Ethan Staddon, suffering an ACL. But for director of rugby Pat Lam having a number of senior players back at his disposal has provided the freshness akin to that of new signings.

Fly-half MacGinty picked a severe Achilles injury in the opening game 12 months ago and did not play again last season. The USA international should have got the score moving on his return with an early penalty, only to pull his effort badly wide of the sticks - much to his own disgust.

That came back to haunt the visitors as Cowan-Dickie went over

Bristol thought they had responded when some smart opportunism from Rees-Zammit - in taking a quick lineout after the ball had squirmed past Tom O'Flaherty - put Scotland full-back Tom Jordan over, but that was ruled out as Sharks winger O'Flaherty had not touched the ball.

Rees-Zammit did get his try moments later after a big floated pass from James Williams gave him an easy finish.

A George Ford penalty pushed Sale's advantage to five points, but Rees-Zammit's second try brought his side level when he produced an acrobatic finish from Jordan's zipped pass.

James Williams' three-pointer had Bristol ahead and some fine sniping from scrum-half Randall saw him burrow over to give his side a 10-point cushion at the break.

O'Flaherty produced a nice finish to quickly bring Sale back into things in the second half but despite some belligerent home defending near their own line, Randall grabbed his second of the game.

A thrilling break from explosive Fiji back-row forward Elia Canakaivata on his Prem debut broke open the play and although he was brought down, O'Flaherty eventually finished off the move and it was a three-point game heading into the final 10 minutes.

But the Bears forwards produced the decisive move of the game as their driving maul overpowered their opponents with Gwilliam the man to get the ball down.

Sale tried to respond to the restored 10-point deficit but when Ford missed a penalty in the 79th minute, their hopes of a losing bonus-point and clawing their way back to parity had gone.

Bristol Bears director of rugby Pat Lam told BBC Radio Bristol:

"I'm pleased for the guys because they got some evidence of what they put into pre-season.

"Everyone wants to be better every day and they got their rewards for it. It gives them a lot of confidence heading into next week.

(On what pleased him most): "The workrate. Defensively yes, there's physicality but one area we've really worked on is boys getting back in the game and really helping their mates. That's an area we continue to work on, but we won the physical battle today."

title: Lynn remaining positive despite Wales' USA setback
description: Head coach Sean Lynn is still seeing the positives despite Wales' narrow WXV defeat to USA.
fullText:
Head coach Sean Lynn says he is still seeing the positives despite Wales' narrow WXV defeat to USA.

Wales had gone into the game full of confidence after their eight-try mauling of South Africa, but failed to produce a repeat performance in front of the Cardiff Arms Park faithful.

The first half was encouraging enough, with Wales clawing back a 14-point deficit, but hopes of a second-half resurgence were short-lived amid a string of individual errors that allowed The Eagles to emerge 26-24 winners.

But as Wales head into their week off ahead of next month's double-header against Japan, Lynn said he has seen enough progress.

"I saw some grit, I saw some effort there," he told BBC Sport.

"Before, when we were 21-7 down, I would have seen heads drop, but we're in a good place and came back. Now it's about us learning how to see games off and going back to the simple things we're doing well."

USA edge past Wales in WXV with Tafuna hat-trick

As it happened: USA earn slender WXV series win over Wales

Lynn had hopes of making it three wins on the bounce after the summer's victory over the Barbarians, but saw Wales fall agonisingly short against a side ranked five places above them at sixth in the world.

"When we came into it [pre-season] at the start of July, we said we're going to be a competitive 80-minute team... we did that today," he said.

"Shame we just didn't come up with the penalty, maybe at the end, but we needed to be better elsewhere around the park.

"We need to look at ourselves and individual errors; we can't play Test match rugby if we make those individual errors, and we all know that.

"We just couldn't keep the ball; we had opportunities to get out of our 22, we had opportunities to go into their 22 and put pressure on."

Wales co-captain Kate Williams was in tears of joy last week, but said the team was "deflated" after their USA showing.

"As a team, we were there at the 60th minute; we just needed to execute and we didn't," she said.

"What happens then is you're just looking at each other, because it's a mistake here, a mistake there; we just needed to come together and do what we're good at, which is being physical and taking it to them.

"This might sound like a big statement, but it didn't feel like a game that they out and out won against us; it felt like a game that we lost, and that's just really frustrating."

Wales will have a week to reflect on such frustrations before returning to camp to prepare for next month's trip to Japan, where they face the Sakura Fifteen in two Tests on 24 and 31 October.

title: Scotland beat NI to boost World Cup qualification hopes
description: Scotland beat Northern Ireland 67-43 to make it two wins from two in the Netball World Cup Qualifier while Wales defeat the Republic of Ireland to keep their hopes alive.
fullText:
Scotland beat Northern Ireland 67-43 to make it two wins from two in the Netball World Cup 2027 qualifying competition at the Playsport Arena in East Kilbride.

The Scots racked up their highest ever score against NI as they boosted their hopes of making next year's tournament in Sydney.

In Saturday's other game, Wales overcame the Republic of Ireland 76-33 to keep alive their hopes of qualification.

The two teams to join England as Europe Regional Qualifiers will be decided on Sunday, with Wales facing Scotland in a key encounter and Northern Ireland playing the Republic of Ireland, with goal average of the matches possibly coming into play.

Friday's opening matches ended with Northern Ireland edging out Wales 50-49 and tournament hosts Scotland getting the better of the Republic of Ireland 84-29.

World-ranked 15 Northern Ireland trailed Scotland 17-13 after the first quarter of what was a feisty, physical encounter on Saturday.

Northern Ireland reduced their deficit by only one goal in the third quarter as the Scots led 47-33 after the third 15 minute period of the match.

Scotland pulled clear in the final quarter to secure victory.

title: GB's Potter takes silver at Triathlon World Series
description: Georgia Taylor-Brown finishes second to France's Cassandre Beaugrand at the World Championship Triathlon Series final, with GB team-mates Kate Waugh and Beth Potter in third and fourth respectively.
fullText:
Great Britain's Beth Potter claimed silver at the World Championship Triathlon Series behind Olympic champion Cassandre Beaugrand of France.

The final event of the series took place in Pontevedra, Spain, where Potter needed a win to overhaul Beaugrand in the overall standings.

But she finished fourth, with team-mates Georgia Taylor-Brown and Kate Waugh finishing second and third behind Beaugrand.

Beaugrand won comfortably, completing the 1.5km swim, 40km bike ride and 10km run in one hour 50 minutes 52 seconds, which was over a minute quicker than Taylor-Brown.

Potter, who won the World Series at Pontevedra in 2023, remained in contention at the end of the cycle, but Beaugrand stretched clear of the three Brits in the second lap of the run and held firm.

It concludes a dominant season for Beaugrand, who has won all five of the World Championship circuit races she entered.

Taylor-Brown won the Czech Republic leg of the series earlier this month, which was her first win on the tour since 2023.

title: England's Harrison scores last-gasp try to beat Black Ferns
description: Zoe Harrison scores last-gasp try as England defeat New Zealand at Allianz Stadium to avoid a second successive draw in the WXV Global Series.
fullText:
Tries: Moloney-MacDonald, Kildunne, Breach, Harrison Cons: Harrison 3

Tries: Du Plessis, Leti-I'iga, Paul Cons: Sorensen-McGee 2

Zoe Harrison scored a last-gasp try as England defeated New Zealand at Allianz Stadium to avoid a second successive draw in the WXV Global Series.

With the scores level at 19-19 in the 81st minute and having missed a penalty moments earlier, Harrison intercepted a pass as the Black Ferns tried to counter-attack, the fly-half diving over the line and piled up on by celebrating team-mates.

The world champions' record 39-game winning run came to an end last weekend in the 26-26 draw with Canada, but this week they were able to find a dramatic path to victory, much to the delight of the 59,871 crowd.

New Zealand, the last team to beat England in the World Cup final in 2022, suffered their first defeat under new head coach Whitney Hansen.

The Black Ferns had taken a deserved lead at half-time after tries from Amy du Plessis and Ayesha Leti-I'iga ruled out Claudia Moloney-MacDonald's opening score.

Tries by Ellie Kildunne and Jess Breach - either side of Marlie Packer having to go off for concussion after being hit hard by a high tackle - restored England's lead.

Mererangi Paul's converted try drew the game level on 70 minutes to set up a grandstand finish.

Red Roses embrace growing competitiveness of game

Rugby Union Weekly: Harrison's last-gasp try seals dramatic England win

The Black Ferns have beaten the Red Roses in all five World Cup final meetings they have contested.

Canada outclassed New Zealand in last year's World Cup semi-final to deny a repeat of what is one of rugby's great rivalries.

Under Hansen, who took over as head coach after last year's disappointing World Cup, the Black Ferns were unbeaten and have defeated Canada and France this year.

The world's second-ranked side spent a large chunk of the first half deep in England's 22, and an opportunistic kick found unmarked space for Du Plessis to dot down for a deserved try.

England comfortably beat New Zealand 49-31 in their most recent meeting in 2024, winning all three encounters since their 2022 World Cup final defeat, which has opened the door for Canada to become the Red Roses' toughest contest.

However, the years were rolled back in Twickenham as Hansen's side brought a fearsome level of physicality and speed to challenge the Red Roses.

Leti-I'iga, who had an opening try ruled out, caused havoc throughout the first half and finally crossed after Tyla King broke clear, before a poorly judged cross-field kick, with another try beckoning, let John Mitchell's side off the hook.

England have not led at half-time in any of their Global WXV Series games.

Given their season only began two weeks ago against Australia, Mitchell has been quick to defend his side's rustiness.

Individual magic from Kildunne, who spotted a gap on the wing for her try, and a yellow card for a high shot by Veisinia Mahutariki-Fakalelu, presented Mitchell with an opportunity to empty his bench with momentum behind his side.

Breach's simple finish came in the next play as any fears of a first loss in four years began to dissolve.

But the Black Ferns refused to go away and continued to trouble England's defence, which is now being influenced by coaching consultant Shaun Edwards.

Mitchell's side were criticised for turning down a kickable penalty late in the game against Canada.

The opportunity again presented itself, and Harrison took it on from distance, but the ball came up well short.

Canada opted to kick the ball out and accept the draw last week, which is not in the DNA of New Zealand, and they attacked from distance in an attempt to inflict England's first loss on home soil since 2016.

That proved to be the wrong decision, as a pass was picked off deep inside the visitors' 22, and instead the Red Roses won their 14th straight game at Allianz Stadium.

title: Australia down Scotland with second-half burst
description: Scotland suffer a third successive defeat in the WXV Global Series as clinical Australia prove too strong in Edinburgh.
fullText:
Tries: Gallagher Cons: Nelson Pens: Nelson

Tries: Miller, Wood, Hoy, Moleko Cons: Wood 2 Pens: Wood 2

Scotland suffered a third successive defeat in the WXV Global Series as clinical Australia proved too strong in Edinburgh.

After losses against Canada and New Zealand - ranked two and three in the world - hopes were high the Scots could get off the mark against the side one place below them in the world rankings.

Despite leading 10-5 at the break, Scotland could not live with the rampant Wallaroos, who ran in three tries in a devastating eight-minute second-half spell to secure a comfortable win.

The sides meet again in Sydney next weekend.

Evie Gallagher, following her two tries against New Zealand last weekend, gave Scotland the lead on 15 minutes, dotting down to round off a period of pressure on the Australian line.

The hosts were on top, with Meryl Smith in midfield and lock Holland Bogan carrying hard and asking questions of the Australian defence, but loose work at the line-out cost Dave Butcher's team some promising attacking positions.

The Wallaroos grew into the game as the half wore on and hit back with a well-worked try. Scotland repelled a rolling line-out maul close to their own line, but the visitors remained patient and spun the ball wide for Georgina Friedrichs to put Desiree Miller over in the corner.

The Scots hit back immediately when Australia were penalised for holding on straight from the restart, and Helen Nelson banged over a penalty to give her side a five-point lead at the break.

However, Australia flew out of the blocks after the interval and turned the game on its head with three tries in quick succession.

The first came when a rolling line-out maul was halted just short and scrum-half Samantha Wood was on hand to dive over. She converted her own try to nudge the visitors in front for the first time, and it was a double blow for Scotland as Gallagher was sin-binned for illegally bringing down the initial maul.

With the numerical advantage, the Wallaroos came on strong as Brianna Hoy and then Faitala Moleko cut through to score and put the visitors in charge at 24-10.

Wood knocked over a penalty to put Australia beyond two scores and added another late on to cap off a dominant second half from the Wallaroos.

title: Gloucester shock Exeter for superb victory
description: Gloucester produce an outstanding display in scoring seven tries to win 45-24 at last season's runners-up Exeter Chiefs.
fullText:
Tries: Iosefa-Scott, E Roots, Varney, Gulley Cons: Slade 2

Tries: Loader 2, S Atkinson, Lake 2, Joseph, Denny Cons: C Atkinson 4, Barton

Gloucester delivered an outstanding performance on the first weekend of the new Prem season to stun Exeter Chiefs at Sandy Park.

The Cherry and Whites only once won on the road last term as they finished eighth, but they matched that immediately with this superb showing.

Summer arrival, and new captain and Wales skipper, Dewi Lake led the way with two of their seven tries.

Winger Ben Loader helped himself to two, while Seb Atkinson, a fine solo effort from Will Joseph and a debut try from Junior Denny completed their try haul.

Exeter finished as runners-up last season after losing to Northampton Saints in the final in June, but they were well beaten.

Josh Iosefa-Scott and Ethan Roots grabbed their first-half scores before Stephen Varney and then Louie Gulley ensured they at least managed a bonus point.

After a few years in the doldrums, Exeter had a thrilling spring and summer with their unexpected run to The Prem final at Twickenham. With new American investment at Sandy Park, hopes are high about the direction of travel in Devon but this was a rude awakening to the new season for Rob Baxter's team.

The Cherry and Whites had a miserable campaign in limping home in eighth and they have not reached the play-offs for seven years, but the acquisition of Wales pair Lake and Jac Morgan has increased belief for the new campaign.

That was in evidence in their positive start as they worked the ball from one corner to the other, with Ben Redshaw's kick bouncing up perfectly for Loader to finish.

A sustained spell of phases eventually resulted in Iosefa-Scott driving over from close range for the hosts before a smart kick over the top from scrum-half Caolan Englefield allowed England centre Atkinson to win a foot race and touch down as Gloucester regained the lead.

Loader's second try extended that advantage as he showed impressive footwork to conjure up another fine kick towards the left corner and dive over.

Gloucester had produced an impressive opening half, but Roots grabbed a second try for the hosts as the flanker found himself on the wing with nobody able to stop his charge.

However, there was still time for the men from Kingsholm to secure a bonus point by the break as captain Lake brilliantly went over in the corner after he had turned down a kick at goal to earn a 26-12 interval lead

Lake's influence in his new team was there for all to see as he was at the back of a driving maul to grab his second try for a dominant Gloucester.

Joseph then scored the try of the game with a brilliant burst of speed from inside his own half that took him outside and inside three defenders.

Varney quickly grabbed Exeter's third try and with visiting flanker Freddie Thomas sin-binned for the final 10 minutes, replacement hooker Gulley went over on his Prem debut to ensure the Chiefs at least claimed a bonus point.

However, that debut try was matched by 18-year-old winger Denny, who scored with the last play of the game to seal Gloucester's first win in Devon since 2015.

Exeter Chiefs director of rugby Rob Baxter told BBC Radio Devon:

"We were actually quite poor today. We didn't have a lot of ambition into the wind, we kicked quite poorly and at times when we didn't even need to - we didn't even look to counter.

"I thought Gloucester were good. They were clinical, they looked powerful at times and we lacked in composure and how we wanted to attack the game.

"We could easily have got back to having two points and two points might make a massive difference. That's why I am really genuinely frustrated because we are so much better than we showed."

Gloucester director of rugby George Skivington told BBC Radio Gloucestershire:

"We've talked a lot about behaviours and standards and what we're going after this season, but there's a really special group and we felt that all through pre-season.

"It's really easy to say but what they showed on the pitch today is a great starting point for us.

"Regardless of the result, some of the behaviours - particularly in that second half - when we were down a man and going through 30 phases of defence, bodies on the line, getting up and going again, is testament to the lads, and what they're willing to give."

title: 'Mr Saturday' Russell 'comes through other side after real tough period'
description: George Russell described the Azerbaijan Grand Prix as "the most dominant weekend I've had in my career" after a win that felt like vindication.
fullText:
For George Russell, this one felt like vindication, proof that he had "come through the other side" and was back to his best after what he acknowledged was a "real tough period" during this Formula 1 season.

The Mercedes driver's victory in the Azerbaijan Grand Prix, holding off Red Bull's Max Verstappen in one of the closest finishes in history, was his first since the end of June - seven races ago.

In that time, team-mate Kimi Antonelli has won three times, to take his tally of victories to eight for the season.

So Russell needed this, his third victory, in a year that he started as championship favourite. Instead, Antonelli has taken the season by the throat and all but crushed the life out of Russell's hopes.

Now, though, a glimmer of hope still exists for Russell, even if he is too realistic to think too much about it for now.

His win, combined with Antonelli's fifth place after what the Italian admitted was his "worst weekend of the year in terms of performance", has cut the points gap between them to 66.

That's still huge, with either seven or eight races still to go, and 25 points for a win. But it's a lot better than the 81-point margin Russell faced before Baku.

"My team-mate's had an incredible season," Russell said. "He's been pretty flawless throughout, but now we're getting to crunch time.

"But I'm just going to focus on myself. You know, if I continue delivering performances like I've done this weekend, no matter what happens towards the end of the season, I'll be happy."

With the grand prix brought forward 24 hours from the usual Sunday slot, it was an appropriate result for a man whose prowess in qualifying has earned him the nickname 'Mr Saturday'.

Russell wins despite late Verstappen challenge

Russell faultless and Hadjar excellent on return - driver ratings

Russell has been through the mill in 2026. He dominated the intra-team battle last year, but the tables have turned dramatically this season, as Antonelli felt immediately at home in the new Mercedes after the biggest rule changes in F1 history, and the Briton very much did not.

For Russell, the blows have kept coming. Every apparent revival was met with another setback. Every time he felt he had made progress, Antonelli's apparently effortless way of extracting that little bit more from the car chastened him.

No experience was more painful than the Italian Grand Prix at Monza two races ago, when Russell started from the front row, and Antonelli 19th after a grid penalty.

Russell knew it was a golden opportunity to make up ground. Instead, it was Antonelli who won the race, with what will go down as one of the greatest drives in history. Russell looked on the verge of tears after that one.

But he kept the belief, and in Baku it all came together.

Russell was a man on a mission all weekend, fastest from the moment he took to the track, while Antonelli, after losing half the two hours of practice on the first day, lost his cool.

He made a mistake in qualifying, took a wheel off on an inside wall, and started 16th. There was to be no repeat of Monza, even if fifth was a very creditable comeback result.

"I felt always a step behind," Antonelli said, "and especially with the mistake in qualifying the confidence level was not high and today was about damage limitation.

"Just probably also the mindset was not in the best place. I wasn't there. I wasn't really present, especially with what happened so early on and just didn't take the same risks, especially after qualifying.

"Today was more damage-safe mode instead of full attack. I just make sure next weekend we get back in the right level."

If he does, this will go down as a blip in an otherwise stunningly impressive breakthrough season by a potential future great. But the parallels with last year are unavoidable.

In 2025, McLaren's Oscar Piastri arrived in Azerbaijan apparently in control of the championship, and possessing a big lead over team-mate Lando Norris, albeit less than half what Antonelli's is now.

But Piastri had some kind of meltdown on the streets of Baku, what he described after arriving back in the city this week as "the worst race of my career".

And after that, the wheels came off for the Australian, and he was overtaken by the end of the year not only by Norris, but also by Verstappen.

There is no reason to believe Antonelli will suffer the same fate. But he still has something to process in the few days before taking to the track again in Malaysia on Friday.

This was the first time Russell has produced a weekend like this all year, when he was simply superior. Before, even when he won, Antonelli was right there with him, sometimes even faster.

How did Russell do this? It has taken hard work and analysis on his part and with his engineers.

He hasn't been comfortable in this year's car, feeling it does not suit his driving style, so he has had to put in the effort to make the driving feel natural. And he feels he is finally getting somewhere.

Deputy team principal Bradley Lord said: "He had some difficult moments before the summer break, some soul-searching as well at points, and he's come back really strong, focused on the driving, focusing on the essentials of what he needs to do to put his weekends together step by step."

Russell said: "I'm very proud of the resilience that I and my close group of engineers have shown during the tough periods this year because there's been a lot of hard work to overcome some of the challenges, to adapt my driving style to suit this new car better.

"And F1 is so tough, you don't get opportunities to practise this, and finally it's coming to me a bit more intuitively than it once did, and I'm gaining confidence. And especially on circuits like this, it just allows you to eke out that little bit more on the brakes, get that little bit closer to the walls, and it's been a flawless weekend.

"It's been four races since the (summer) break. I've been on the front row in three of them, three podiums from the four races. I feel I can fight for victory week in, week out now."

Norris says Colapinto should be banned after accident

Azerbaijan GP Review: Vettel Gives His Verdict

The win was looking comfortable for a while, as he romped away at the front in the first stint while Piastri delayed Verstappen.

But two mid-race safety cars closed up the field and left Verstappen right on Russell's tail.

Russell could not shake him off, but he continued to be flawless. Even when slowing for a yellow flag on the final lap caused a loss of turbo boost pressure and left him vulnerable on the run to the flag.

"It's for sure the most dominant weekend I've had in my career," Russell said. "So that has come at a really great moment. And also to achieve it on a circuit that requires so much commitment and confidence, I'm really proud of, because it would have been very easy for me to lose the faith this season."

Mercedes have lost their early season dominance over the summer, but the Bahrain/Malaysia race will see their first big upgrade for a while.

"I'm really excited," Russell said. "That's going to be a good step forward.

"Our car has been working exceptionally well on the low-drag circuits. We've got a really efficient car, so here at Baku we've been exceptionally fast. But I think from next week onwards, we're hoping to make a bigger step to the rest of the field. But nothing's sure until we see how it pans out in reality."

And even if Antonelli cannot be anything but still a strong favourite, the same goes for the championship.

"There's much less pressure on me than there is on him," Russell said. "Yesterday was probably his first mistake of this whole season in a proper session, qualifying, race, and he still came home in P5 today.

"I didn't really consider myself in this fight for a number of races, purely because my performance wasn't strong enough.

"Now I feel like if the season were to have started today, or since the summer break, you know, I feel very much I would have been able to fight.

"Now I've got this big deficit. It can change quick. So I'm not chasing that. I'm chasing to win every race, and what will be, will be."

title: Gilmour catalyst, impressive Welsh, but same issue for Scotland?
description: BBC Sport Scotland picks out what we learned from Sebastien Pocognoli's first game in charge as Scotland drew with Slovenia.
fullText:
New head coach Sebastien Pocognoli said his Scotland bow against Slovenia was "two games in the same game" as his side claimed a Nations League point after a much-improved second half showing.

The Scots struggled in a disjointed first half, but took control of the game in the second period and created enough chances to win, but had to settle for a 0-0 draw.

"First half, was not what we expected in terms of structure, " Pocognoli told BBC Scotland.

"We were in between for the press, actually we were a little bit surprised about the formation of Slovenia, but at half-time we fixed this and you can see that the second half was much better.

"We produced what we wanted to show every minute, but first half we learned to stick together, to defend the box, to be resilient and to be patient to change the game."

There were two debuts in Ljubljana, a return for Oli McBurnie, and a change of shape after seven years of Steve Clarke ended after the World Cup in the summer.

It is only the first of four games in this international window, but here are the key takeaways from Pocognoli's debut.

Scotland begin Pocognoli era with encouraging Slovenia draw

'Eternally grateful' McBurnie ready to show what Scotland have missed

Napoli midfielder Billy Gilmour missed the World Cup campaign after a heartbreaking injury against Curacao in Scotland's final home warm-up game.

He returned to the heart of midfield alongside Lewis Ferguson and, according to former Scotland midfielder John Collins was "the catalyst for everything" in the second half.

"Straight from the start of the second half he was getting the ball, playing forward passes and following his pass to the strikers," Collins said.

Gilmour played further up the pitch than Ferguson, "close to a creative 10" according to former Scotland winger Pat Nevin, and played 32 passes into the final third, more than any player on the pitch.

The former Chelsea man combined well with McBurnie on the edge of the box to set up a shot for himself; he slipped in Robbie Ure who opted to cross rather than shoot; and picked out Kieron Bowie with a wonderful through ball which should have resulted in a goal.

Those were just a handful of his key moments. Pocognoli spoke afterwards about the half-time tweak to bring Gilmour deeper to make it harder for Slovenia to play through them and have greater control of the ball.

"We fixed the position of Billy to be a little bit lower and to have Oli McBurnie a little bit 

"Also, that creates some imbalance in the defence from Slovenia, where we can go through the lines with a good chance of Billy or through the depth with the chance of Kieron Bowie or with some crosses.

"He's a fantastic player, I really like him. He's a creative player who always looks forward, always ready to find a solution with a clear game plan, also a good presence around the box and also very good defensively."

Swansea City defender Stephen Welsh was one of two debutants in Slovenia, playing on the left of a back three despite being right footed.

Scotland struggled defensively at times in the first half, with Slovenia playing over the top of them, but Welsh's positioning after the break also helped change the game.

In the first half, his average position was short of the halfway line, but by the end of the game it was in Slovenian territory.

His most common pass went from being to his fellow centre-back Scott McKenna, to Andy Robertson at wing-back.

"It was the starting position of the back three for which changed it - they were in a really good starting position," former Scotland defender Callum Davidson told BBC Scotland.

"In the first half they were quite deep and worried about the ball over the top. But we managed to nullify that and then keep the ball."

The former Motherwell and Celtic defender created a clear goalscoring chance with a wonderful through ball to Bowie, and he finished the game with 16 passes into the final third and the highest accuracy rating.

More aggressive play from Welsh helped set the tone after the break, as he looked assured on his international debut.

With a new manager, injuries to Che Adams and Lawrence Shankland, and on the back of his strong form with Hull City, Oli McBurnie made his first Scotland appearance since 2021 in attack.

Ure, fresh from his move from Sirius in Sweden to Sevilla, made his debut while Sassuolo's Kieron Bowie came off the bench in the second half.

Those three have one club goal between them this season - Bowie's against Juventus - and none for Scotland in their limited caps.

All three were presented chances to score in the second half, though. McBurnie nicked possession and when through, but failed to round Jan Oblak in the Slovenia goal.

His header from a corner was also beaten away by the Atletico Madrid's goalkeeper. Ure drove a low shot off the post in the first half from outside the box, a difficult chance, but then later opted to go for a cut back when slipped in by Gilmour.

Bowie ended with the highest expected goals rating in the Scotland team (0.94) despite playing only 25 minutes - after twice staring at the whites of Oblak's eyes and failing to find the net.

It is only one game, and Scotland will not face a goalkeeper of Oblak's quality in every match, but there is a lingering concern about the national side's goalscoring ability - they have managed one in their last four competitive games.

For all the positives the attackers brought in the second half in general play, do Scotland have someone with a killer instinct?

"International level is all about taking your chances, you don't get too many," Davidson said.

"It's about being really clinical, so for these strikers it's important when you get games like this to take your chances. That's the disappointment from today."

title: England embrace growing competitiveness of women's game
description: England edge past New Zealand with a last-gasp try by Zoe Harrison as they embrace the growing competitiveness of women's rugby.
fullText:
Winning had been the only currency known to John Mitchell's Red Roses.

From his arrival midway through the 2023 WXV1 campaign to winning the Women's Rugby World Cup for the first time in 11 years, England won every single game.

However, their record 39-game run of victories was finally halted by Canada, last year's World Cup finalists, in a thrilling 26-26 draw at Sandy Park last week.

Welcoming New Zealand, unbeaten under new head coach Whitney Hansen, to Allianz Stadium brought a feeling of jeopardy that had not been felt for a very long time.

Despite Mitchell openly stating that the WXV Global Series, with no trophy at the end of it, would provide new opportunities, losing in front of a 59,871 crowd at the home of English rugby would not have been part of the long-term development plan.

When Braxton Sorensen-McGee, with less than 10 minutes remaining, landed a tough conversion to bring the Black Ferns level at 19-19, the Red Roses once again found themselves in a sticky situation.

Unlike last week, they came up clutch as Zoe Harrison redeemed herself for a late penalty miss by snatching victory with an intercept try in the final play.

Given the clock was in overtime, England do have to count themselves lucky that New Zealand attempted to run from deep and gifted them a winning score.

"We couldn't have a repeat of what happened against Canada last week. A draw wasn't good enough, so we had to get the points somehow," Harrison told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"It's massive - it goes back to that World Cup final [in 2022] for me - beating them on home soil was fantastic and it being such a close game is great for women's rugby."

Rugby Union Weekly: Harrison's last-gasp try seals dramatic England win

New Zealand, the world's second-ranked side, remain the last team to defeat the Red Roses at the World Cup final in 2022.

Leading 12-7 at half-time, ending that unbeaten run looked a real possibility.

This campaign, England have lacked the same clinical edge that saw them become world champions.

Their defence, now supported by coaching legend Shaun Edwards, has also been leaky. But they are without a number of key players, including World Cup-winning captain Zoe Stratford.

"To put it into context, the Red Roses don't play New Zealand and Canada often - it's important to learn how to win tight Test matches," Mitchell said.

"The message at half-time was that this game will turn - we will get some possession and let's attack it.

"The girls took the handbrake off and tried to go to space, even from deep, and were still tenacious without the ball, which was awesome."

Running from 2026 to 2028, the new WXV Global Series features the world's top 12 teams and is designed to provide more competitive matches before the 2029 World Cup.

England have already faced the world's second and third-ranked sides and now travel to Canada to complete their three-Test series against the World Cup runners-up.

"The game is getting better and better and we are just trying to make that gap bigger," Red Roses captain Meg Jones said.

"We know there are going to be close games and we will compete as hard as we can."

New Zealand have beaten England in five World Cup finals and were once the undisputed number one team in the world.

That dominance has faded in recent years, particularly after their failure to reach last year's World Cup final.

Despite a fourth straight defeat by the Red Roses, it is clear under Hansen that the Black Ferns are trending in the right direction.

That comes after increased investment in the domestic game, with Super Rugby Aupiki operating as a fully professional, full-time competition for the first time this year.

"We didn't want a draw," New Zealand head coach Whitney Hansen said.

"After watching last week [against Canada], we knew we were going to fight to the death, so I love that she threw that pass.

"I think for us, win or lose, we're about our performance. We've talked heaps about what does great look like - where have we achieved that and where haven't we?"

Next year, the British and Irish Lions women's team will tour New Zealand for the first time.

A competitive series is essential to the success of the tour.

Prior to last year's epic finale at Allianz Stadium, England - likely to make up a large portion of the Lions squad - comfortably beat New Zealand 49-31 in their most recent meeting in 2024.

"People are starting to realise the context we are in. Even if we had lost, we were right up there," Mitchell added.

"New Zealand are in a really great position for the Lions series and heading in the right direction for the [2027] World Cup. We are also evolving [as a team]."

Blowing away every team comfortably or being pushed to the limit to win a Test - which would England prefer?

"This is what living feels like," Jones declared.

Games in October against Toronto and Ottawa, with the series perfectly poised at 1-1, should give them those feelings again.

This was only the third game of the season for Mitchell's players, but being pushed all the way is something that he and his side are loving and embracing.

Despite all that, an undefeated run spanning four years has been extended further.
