title: Republic of Ireland to wear black armbands for Israel game
description: Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, after confirming they will go ahead with the fixture.
fullText:
Republic of Ireland players intend to wear black armbands "in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict" for Sunday's Nations League game against Israel in Hungary, after confirming they will go ahead with the fixture.

Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell confirmed one player has withdrawn from the squad before the match.

But he added that a vote among the squad produced a "significant majority" in favour of playing.

As well as the intention to wear black armbands for Sunday's 'away' game against Israel in Debrecen, Courell said the players will make further gestures for the initial game and the return 'home' fixture against Israel next Sunday in Serbia.

The fixtures have been embroiled in controversy since the two teams were drawn to play each other in Group B3.

Republic of Ireland players faced calls to withdraw from the games because of the ongoing Israel-Gaza war with a "Stop The Game" campaign - organised by the pressure group Irish Sport for Palestine - gathering pace.

"One of their requests is to remove their media obligations for the remainder of this window," Courell said at Saturday's delayed news conference.

"They also have the intention to wear black armbands in recognition of all lives lost in the [Gaza] conflict.

"There will be elements of the pre-match ceremony not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland and it is also the intention of the players to make a significant contribution to charitable donation by virtue of both [Israel] match fees and also the fixture against Austria at the Aviva [Stadium in Dublin on Thursday]."

There appeared to be real doubt on Saturday morning whether the fixture would take place.

A pre-match news conference with manager Heimir Hallgrimsson and a player, scheduled for 09:15 BST, was postponed just 15 minutes before it was scheduled to start, with reporters informed it would instead take place after the team's training session which was also delayed.

The players were locked in a meeting back at their hotel after it emerged a player, believed to be goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, withdrew from the game in protest with several other expressing their concerns about fielding.

Around 13:00 BST, players began to filter out of the meeting room, with it then confirmed the news conference would indeed go ahead, back at Nagyerdei Stadion at 14:30, with training to follow.

More than five hours after the initial news conference was scheduled to begin, Courell - flanked by Hallgrimsson and FAI director of football John Martin - confirmed a players' vote passed by a "significant majority" to play the game.

"This morning, a player expressed their discomfort at the fixture and indicated their intent to withdraw," Courell said.

"This new variable required time for the rest of the squad to consider and what proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly among the players, but also at times with coaching staff and the [FAI] executive.

"There were a lot of positions presented and the association is fully respectful of everyone's right to their respective opinion."

Former Republic of Ireland manager Brian Kerr and ex-international James McClean are among those to have backed calls for a boycott of the fixtures.

The armed Palestinian group Hamas attacked Israel on 7 October 2023, killing about 1,200 people and taking 251 hostages.

In response, Israel launched a massive military offensive in Gaza, during which more than 73,000 people have been killed, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the United Nations.

Hallgrimsson relayed that nobody "can understand the pressure that has been going on these players" and said the lengthy meeting on Saturday stemmed from "a change of mind for one of the players to play the game".

"All of the rest of the players are training today," he confirmed.

"The balance [to play] changed with this [withdrawal] and obviously it was an ongoing discussion but we came to a conclusion and the game is going ahead.

"We will train and there will probably be more discussions tonight and probably tomorrow. It's a unique situation and we are just trying to limit the damage."

The Republic of Ireland lost their opening Nations League fixture in Kosovo on Thursday, a match overshadowed in the build-up by the Israel games.

Asked whether the far from ideal preparation for Sunday's game would affect the players, the Irish boss said "we will see".

"Nobody is comfortable but it's about limiting the damage, both personally and for Irish football, that we need to find some solution on it," Hallgrimsson added.

"There is no action we do that everyone will agree to, so we need to find a solution to limit the damage for us as a group, for Ireland as a nation and the association for football in Ireland.

"We don't know the consequences if we don't play the game but a lot of players share a common feeling, so there are two choices and both are tough. It's a situation you can't win."

title: No Premier League appetite to strip Man City of titles - but threat remains
description: After being found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges for breaching Premier League, could Manchester city really be stripped of eight trophies?
fullText:
It is one of the biggest talking points from the Manchester City case.

Should City be stripped of the eight trophies they won between 2009 and 2018, the period in which they were accused of breaking Premier League financial rules?

Judging by social media, many fans of rival clubs are now hoping for such an outcome.

However BBC Sport has been told there has been little appetite from within the Premier League - both the organisation and clubs - for past titles to be stripped from City

Not quite, as the decision will be made by an independent panel which is yet to hold a "sanction hearing". That means it cannot be ruled out, although a points deduction, huge fine or possibly even expulsion from the Premier League are thought to be more likely.

Here, BBC Sport analyses this difficult issue and decision the panel is now facing.

Man City and the 115 charges - key questions answered

Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict

Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City

"I think we still have a chance to win that league… and then they have to pay me the bonus and give me the medal."

It was almost two years ago that Jose Mourinho mischievously raised the possibility that his former club Manchester United could be handed the 2018 Premier League title held by Manchester City.

Under Mourinho, United finished second to City by 19 points in 2018, his final full campaign in charge at Old Trafford.

City have always denied wrongdoing. But now we know they have been found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges, was Mourinho right?

Premier League rules do not directly make reference to such a sanction, with a fine, points deduction or expulsion listed as possible punishments. However, they also allow for a disciplinary commission panel to impose a penalty "as it shall think fit". That theoretically could include retrospectively-applied points deductions, or the stripping of titles.

Many will argue that if upheld after any appeal, the nature and scale of the wrongdoing City have been found guilty of warrants such as sanction on the basis that titles were won unfairly, and any misrepresentation of revenue and costs gave them a crucial competitive advantage.

City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centred around claims that they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent football's financial rules.

So with a cloud hanging over the trophy-laden era City have enjoyed since the takeover of the club by Abu Dhabi billionaire Sheikh Mansour in 2008, could asterisks now be applied to the titles City won during the period in which they have been found to have broken the rules?

Could they be left blank? Or, as implied by Mourinho, reallocated to those teams who finished runners-up to City?

Such a move would threaten to open the proverbial can of worms, raising questions over other accomplishments.

For instance, there is now scepticism towards the various trophies Chelsea won in the 2010s, after the club were found to have made a catalogue of secret payments to agents over transfers, between 2011 and 2018.

Some will ask that if retrospective action is applied to City, should the same not happen to Chelsea?

It is impossible to know exactly to what extent City benefited on the field from their rule breaches. And which players they may not have been able to afford if they had adhered to the regulations.

And what about the period between December 2018 and February 2023, when City stand accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations?

Should retrospective action be applied then too? Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola's City twice during that time, by a single point in both 2019 and 2022. Last year, the German coach joked he would host a party in his garden if his former club were suddenly awarded those titles.

Some will conclude that the rule breaches between 2009 and 2018 helped City to lay the foundations on which Guardiola built on to achieve so much success, culminating in the Treble triumph of 2023.

Does that era come into scope? Where does it end?

For some, the mass reallocation of titles over such a long period would risk making a mockery of Premier League history, jeopardising its reputation and commercial viability. Others would argue that some 17 years after the first alleged breach, and with City accused of distorting the competition over multiple seasons, serious damage has already been done to the league's standing.

And while there is no Premier League precedent, such concerns have not prevented such punishments being applied before in football. Juventus had the Serie A titles they won in 2005 and 2006 revoked as a result of the Calciopoli match-fixing scandal - when five Italians teams were penalised for attempting to influence results by picking certain referees. The first title was left blank by authorities, with the second reallocated to Inter Milan.

There is also a British precedent. Elgin City won the 1992-93 Highland League, but were later stripped of the title after having been found to have fielded ineligible players.

There are examples in other sports too. In 2012, Lance Armstrong was stripped of his seven Tour de France titles by the UCI, cycling's governing body, for doping. And the reallocation of medals has become commonplace in athletics as a result of positive drugs tests that can emerge long after events have taken place.

In cases such as City's, involving financial rule breaches, the argument for such a punishment is more complicated. Many will see it as unfair that players and fans unconnected to any rule breaches should suffer by losing titles.

And with some suggesting that relations between the United Arab Emirates and the UK could be put under serious pressure by this ruling, one can only imagine the diplomatic tensions if past titles were then taken away from the club.

On Friday, former City midfielder Rodri dismissed talk of the club being stripped of some of the titles they won.

"What we did, they cannot take out of us," he added.

"It's something that is not paid by money. It's paid with effort, with the damage, with, you know, being shoulder to shoulder every day.

"I can tell you that everything was deserved, and I'm glad that I could live one of the best eras of English football in here."

Others, however, will insist the rewriting of history is the only way of restoring the competition's official record, and rewarding clubs that competed within the rules.

In terms of retrospective action, the compensation claims for lost earnings that several clubs are known to be considering launching against City are more likely than the stripping of titles.

A lawyer told me: "The question isn't whether the clubs can take legal action... it's: Where does the line of people who have a case actually end?

"The clubs who didn't win/qualify/stay up; the players who didn't get bonuses, contract extensions; the staff who missed out on bonuses; the agents who didn't get their uplift on their player deals...

"It's endless and potentially so destructive to the whole ecosystem."

Whatever happens, more division and disruption seems guaranteed.

title: Trump labels Hormuz 'Trump Strait' after Iran offers conditions to reopen waterway
description: U.S. President Donald Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if the U.S. meets certain conditions.
fullText:
U.S. President Donald Trump on Saturday rejected Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within a week if the U.S. meets certain conditions.

Trump spoke to reporters Saturday outside the White House before leaving for a college football game.

Iran offered this week to reopen the strait and resume talks on its nuclear program in seven days if the U.S. lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observes a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.

Meanwhile, Iranian media outlets say the country's president has left New York after the United Nations gathering of world leaders that included Iran's indirect talks with the United States. And Saudi Arabia says it has intercepted another missile it blames on Iran -backed Houthis in neighboring Yemen.

Here is a look at the latest news from the Middle East on Saturday. More coverage of the U.N. General Assembly is available here.

Trump posted an image early Saturday morning on his Truth Social platform of the Strait of Hormuz labeled "Trump Strait," in the first public indication of his thinking after Iran proposed the new deal and suggested it might help Trump ahead of the midterm elections.

The White House on Friday said only that U.S. officials were having positive and constructive conversations with mediators on the Iran war. Earlier in the week, Iran held hours of indirect talks with the U.S.

Semiofficial media outlets in Iran reported that President Masoud Pezeshkian has departed New York for Tehran after the annual U.N. gathering of world leaders.

Pezeshkian's speech to the gathering pushed back against Trump's latest threat to "annihilate" the Islamic Republic, but he ended by saying Tehran remains open to diplomacy.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told journalists Friday night that under Tehran's proposal, Iran would reopen the Strait of Hormuz and resume talks on its nuclear program in seven days if the United States lifts its naval blockade of Iranian ports, waives sanctions on Iranian oil sales and observes a ceasefire that would include Lebanon.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian told CBS that from his viewpoint as a physician, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei has "no specific ongoing health issues" despite not being seen or heard in public since the war with the U.S. and Israel began in February.

In the transcript CBS released, Pezeshkian described his most recent meeting with Khamenei as lasting over seven hours. "But, of course, he was healthy enough to be able to withstand those hours of that situation. From a medical standpoint, he's completely healthy," the president said. When asked whether the supreme leader's face and legs have recovered, Pezeshkian responded, "Yes."

Khamenei's father and other family members were killed on the opening day of the war.

Saudi Arabia's military spokesperson, Maj. Gen. Turki al-Malki, claimed early Saturday that a ballistic missile launched by the Iran-backed Houthi rebels in neighboring Yemen was intercepted and destroyed. He said it was fired toward the southwestern city of Khamis Mushait.

The Associated Press couldn't immediately verify that independently. There was no immediate statement of responsibility, though it can take days for the Houthis to issue one.

A regional body representing Arab Gulf states, the Gulf Cooperation Council, condemned the latest Houthi attacks as a "grave escalation and threat to regional security" and urged the international community to respond.

Iraq said it is in direct contact with the U.S. to secure exemptions from sanctions on Iranian airlines as Washington continues economic pressure on Tehran.

The Iraqi prime minister's office said the aim is to get exemptions for certain airports, noting flights for humanitarian reasons such as medical treatment, education and religious pilgrimages.

Many pilgrims in neighboring Iran visit sites such as Karbala and Najaf.

Israeli settlers have intensified efforts to seize natural springs and heritage sites in the occupied West Bank. The springs are vital for drinking water, tourism and agriculture and increasingly inaccessible to the 2.8 million Palestinians living there.

In the Jordan Valley, settlers cut a water pipe to a Palestinian village, redirecting it to a pool they named after Herod, the Roman-appointed king of Judea. Israeli rights groups say the move is part of a broader effort to claim heritage sites.

The struggle for water access highlights the ongoing contest for control of the West Bank, where Palestinians have faced shortages since 1967.

This report will be updated throughout the day as new developments emerge.

title: Where to watch Texas at Tennessee: Time, TV channel, streaming
description: Find out the time, TV schedule, streaming info and more for the Texas Longhorns SEC opener at the Tennessee Volunteers at Neyland Stadium.
fullText:
The Texas Longhorns go on the road for the first time this year, as they travel to Knoxville, Tennessee to face the Volunteers at Neyland Stadium. The Longhorns are the No. 1 team in the nation in both the Coaches and AP polls, while the Vols are No. 13 in the Coaches Poll and No. 14 in the AP rankings.

The game will be a borderline circus, with ESPN College GameDay on hand, Johnny Knoxville as the guest picker, President Donald Trump in attendance and half-off alcohols says before the game at Neyland.

Circus or not, this game is vitally important for Texas' title aspirations. The Longhorns lost their SEC opener last season at Florida and it put them behind the eight-ball all year, eventually missing the college football playoff.

Texas quarterback Arch Manning hopes to change his fortunes on the road. Manning has never won a true road game in regulation and is 2-3 overall.

Streaming options: ESPN app | Fubo (free trial)

Watch Texas vs. Tennessee on Fubo TV! (Regional restrictions may apply)

We're really going to see how much improved the 2026 version of the Texas Longhorns are compared to last year's version. Much of that begins and ends with Arch Manning.

In his career so far, Manning has not been great on the road. He has played five true road games as the Texas starting QB. His record is 2-3. The two wins needed overtime at two of the worst teams in the SEC last year.

Arch has really only looked good this season for a quarter and a half. Granted that was a heck of a quarter and a half as he led an epic comeback over then No. 1 Ohio State. He's also dealt with some controversy this year and his demeanor has completely changed.

I must admit, I have a bad feeling about this game.

Final Score: Texas 17, Tennessee 24

title: Why is F1 Azerbaijan Grand Prix taking place on Saturday?
description: F1 heads to the Baku City Circuit for round 15 of the 2026 season in the Azerbaijani capital
fullText:
F1 returns to the Baku City Circuit for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix this weekend and round 15 of the 2026 season.

Kimi Antonelli continued his brilliant form at the Spanish Grand Prix last time out, winning the first event held on the new Madrid street track after benefiting from a well-timed safety car period early on. Antonelli now leads the world championship by 81 points over Mercedes teammate George Russell.

Max Verstappen finished second in Madrid with pole-sitter Lando Norris having to settle for third. Lewis Hamilton was forced to retire after a brake issue in his Ferrari car and the Briton now trails Antonelli by a mammoth 101 points with nine rounds remaining.

This year's race in Baku will take place on a Saturday because Sunday, 27 September marks Azerbaijan's Remembrance Day, with the whole schedule shifting forward by one day to avoid a clash with a national day of mourning.

Here's everything you need to know about the Azerbaijan Grand Prix.

The race in Baku is taking place on Saturday to avoid a direct clash with Azerbaijan's Remembrance Day, which takes place on 27 September every year.

It is a national day of mourning dedicated to military personnel of the Azerbaijani Armed Forces who lost their lives during the Second Nagorno-Karabakh War in 2020, when 2,783 soldiers were killed during six weeks of fighting.

It is the first Saturday race since the Las Vegas Grand Prix last year, which is always held on Saturday night in Sin City. The Bahrain and Saudi grands prix in 2024 were also held on Saturdays due to the start of Ramadan.

The change essentially means everything moves forward a day.

The Azerbaijan Grand Prix will be broadcast live on Sky Sports in the United Kingdom. Sky's coverage of Sunday's race starts at 10:30am (BST).

Sky Sports subscribers can watch all the action from Baku on the Sky Go app. If you're not a Sky customer, you can grab a NOWTV Day Pass here to watch without a subscription.

In the United States, every practice, qualifying and race session is streamed on Apple TV this year. You can stream Apple TV for FREE, with Apple TV's seven-day free trial.

title: Real Madrid superstar’s latest injury highlights his alarming fitness record since joining the club
description: Real Madrid fans suffered yet another setback this week when Kylian Mbappe picked up an injury during a UEFA Nations League fixture against Turkiye.The Frenchman looked in discomfort shortly after sco...
fullText:
Real Madrid fans suffered yet another setback this week when Kylian Mbappe picked up an injury during a UEFA Nations League fixture against Turkiye.

The Frenchman looked in discomfort shortly after scoring the winning goal, leading to immediate concerns around the French camp. Even his Real Madrid teammate Arda Guler looked worried.

The true extent of Mbappe's injury has not been determined as of yet. But it is yet another reminder of his poor fitness record since joining the club.

As reported by Mundo Deportivo, the setback marks the seventh injury Mbappe has suffered since arriving at Real Madrid in the summer of 2024.

Mbappe scored the match-winning goal vs Turkiye. (Photo by Burak Kara/Getty Images)

Across that period, the Frenchman has missed 14 matches due to injury, a figure that rises to 17 when including three games missed through gastroenteritis at the Club World Cup. Despite that, he has maintained an impressive availability rate of 88.8%.

The most concerning aspect is the nature of this latest problem. Mbappe injured his left knee against Turkiye, the very same joint that troubled him for several months last season.

He initially tried to continue but was ultimately forced off and has since left the France camp to return to Madrid.

That left knee has been his biggest issue since joining the club, having caused a lengthy absence that stretched across the turn of the year and into the early months of 2026.

Despite the worrying history, the initial noises coming out of the France camp have been reassuring.

Real Madrid will hope to have Mbappe back as soon as possible. (Photo by Burak Kara/Getty Images)

France teammate Rayan Cherki offered an encouraging update, suggesting the problem is not as serious as first feared. "He's fine. At first we were very worried, but then we saw it wasn't anything serious," Cherki said.

Those words will offer some comfort to Real Madrid, who cannot afford to be without their talisman for any significant length of time.

Mbappe has been in sensational form this season, scoring eight goals in eight matches and single-handedly carrying the team on several occasions.

Nonetheless, Real Madrid will take no risks with the forward. He is set to return to the club for further assessment, and his comeback will only be sanctioned once he is fully fit.

title: Calafiori out, Bastoni in: Which changes could Italy make after 2-0 Belgium defeat?
description: Roberto Mancini’s second stint as head coach of the Italy national team began with a 2-0 defeat at home against Belgium on Friday night, and though the boos from a half-empty Stadio Olimpico left a ...
fullText:
Roberto Mancini's second stint as head coach of the Italy national team began with a 2-0 defeat at home against Belgium on Friday night, and though the boos from a half-empty Stadio Olimpico left a sour taste, focus is already beginning to shift towards Monday's test against away against Turkey. So, which changes could the Azzurri potentially make?

Mancini named a squad of 34 players for the extra-long international break in September and early October, and there had been hopes that the returning CT would launch a new-look Italy side following the failure to qualify for the 2026 World Cup earlier this year.

The Italy starting XI for the Nations League MD against Belgium at the Stadio Olimpico in Rome (@azzurri)

There was, however, disappointment from large sections of Azzurri supporters after seeing the team sheets on Friday night, given that Mancini had stuck with a core of players who had played key roles during Italy's unsuccessful World Cup qualification campaign, such as Giovanni Di Lorenzo, Gianluca Mancini, Nicolo Barella, Sandro Tonali and Moise Kean.

La Gazzetta dello Sport suggests that some of these might be left out of the line-up when Italy return to action in just a few days' time, away against Turkey in Bursa.

Following his sending off against Bosnia and Herzegovina in the World Cup play-off final back in March, Inter centre-back Alessandro Bastoni was suspended for Friday night's game against Belgium, and is likely to return to the side against Turkey on Monday. He is likely to return in place of Diego Coppola, although Mancini's place in the team is far from guaranteed either.

MILAN, ITALY – NOVEMBER 16: Alessandro Bastoni of Italy warms up prior to the FIFA World Cup 2026 qualifier match between Italy and Norway at San Siro Stadium on November 16, 2025 in Milan, Italy. (Photo by Marco Luzzani/Getty Images)

Arsenal's Riccardo Calafiori is also likely to be rested when Italy take on Turkey on Monday night. Honest Ahanor and Matteo Ruggeri are the most likely candidates to slot in at left-back if Mancini decides to stick with a back four. Federico Dimarco withdrew from the squad through injury at the start of the week.

The Pink Paper suggests that Michael Kayode could finally be given his full Italy debut in place of Di Lorenzo against Turkey, although this is still not 100% guaranteed.

UDINE – APRIL 18: Nicolò Zaniolo of Udinese looks on during the warm up ahead of the Serie A match between Udinese Calcio and Parma Calcio 1913 at Stadio Friuli on April 18, 2026 in Udine. (Photo by Timothy Rogers/Getty Images)

Assuming that he is fit to play, Nicolo Zaniolo will be pushing for a starting spot in the Azzurri attack on Monday night. He had been in contention to start against Belgium before being left out of the matchday squad.

Elsewhere, Giorgio Scalvini, Davide Frattesi, Nicolo Fagioli, Issa Doumbia and Daniel Maldini are among the players who will be hoping to be brought into the starting XI against Turkey on Monday.

title: First DVD player announced Sept 26, 1996
description: VHS was showing its age and DVD offered benefits all around
fullText:
On September 26, 1996, Toshiba announced the first DVD player, the Toshiba SD-3000. It was released in Japan in November 1996 and initially cost ¥77,000, equivalent to about $770 US. It was the first consumer DVD player in the world, and of course, DVD became the successor to VHS. Ironically, the first DVD player was announced very close to 20 years after the first VHS VCR.

VHS had a good run, and in 1996 it still had about a decade left, but it was showing its age. It didn’t record at the full resolution of either NTSC or PAL video. Arguably in 1976 few people noticed because screens were comparatively small and the VCR connected over RF, causing signal degradation anyway. But by 1996, TV tubes were higher quality, most TVs had at least composite connections and many had higher-quality connections like S-Video or even component video.

From a consumer standpoint, tapes would wear out after repeated viewing and the need to rewind them was a bit of an inconvenience. People of a certain age remember VHS tapes from rental stores like Blockbuster having stickers on them that said, “Be kind, rewind!” to remind them to rewind tapes before returning them. Some stores even charged a fee if you didn’t rewind the tape.

From the TV and movie industry’s standpoint, VHS was a liability because it could record. Getting consumers hooked on a format that didn’t record would unlock potential additional revenue streams. Technology to inhibit copying VHS tapes existed but wasn’t perfect. DVD offered a chance to include copy prevention as part of the design. And the inability to record video from TV meant it would become much easier for studios to sell TV shows on DVD, to get an additional revenue stream beyond syndication.

The upside to consumers was that DVDs would look and sound better than VHS, and be more durable. As long as the disc didn’t scratch or break, it could last nearly forever. DVD resolution was 720×480 in NTSC markets and 720×576 in PAL markets.

DVD wasn’t the first videodisc format. Laserdisc and Capacitance Electronic Disc (CED) were two earlier examples of media that worked on disc, rather than tape. But they were both analog formats, and their discs were larger than CDs, closer in size to vinyl records. DVD would use media the same size as a music CD, and like CD, it would be digital.

There’s nothing particularly special about the Toshiba SD-3000 other than being the first DVD player. It sold in Japan for a few months before giving way to newer models, and I can’t find evidence it was ever exported. Sony started exporting DVD players to other markets, including the United States, in April 1997. In 1997, DVD players ranged in price from about $600 to $1,000, which calculates to about $1,216 to $2,025 in 2026 dollars.

But prices came down quickly. And in 2001, DVD players outsold VCRs. Very inexpensive off-brand DVD players proliferated in the early 2000s, costing as little as $15. At that price, the player cost less than the discs consumers were watching in it. At DVD’s peak, 80% of Americans owned a DVD player.

DVD gave way to Blu-ray in the following decade, as HDTV became more common and showed the limitations of the DVD format. HDTVs could upscale DVD, but Blu-ray encoded at 1920×1080 looked better.

David Farquhar is a computer security professional, entrepreneur, and author. He has written professionally about computers since 1991, so he was writing about retro computers when they were still new. He has been working in IT professionally since 1994 and has specialized in vulnerability management since 2013. He holds Security+ and CISSP certifications. Today he blogs five times a week, mostly about retro computers and retro gaming covering the time period from 1975 to 2000.

title: The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets
description: Trump tries to dominate at the UN as his approval ratings plummet and even some Republicans distance themselves from him
fullText:
Donald Trump stood before the United Nations on Tuesday and threatened to “annihilate” Iran. Yet even as the most powerful man on the planet flexed his military muscles, he was powerless to keep the gravitational pull of domestic politics at bay.

Heading into the UN building in New York, the US president was questioned by Kaitlan Collins, an anchor at CNN, which he had banned from the White House before a judge ruled against him. “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me,” the 80-year-old snapped. “You should not be here covering me.”

The lashing-out was a reminder that even Trump, who has expanded executive power and dominated the national consciousness, finds some things beyond his control. Indeed, 20 months into his second term, there is a widening gap between the president’s self-perceived invincibility and the reality of his waning influence.

Federal courts are reining him in. Congressional Republicans are straying from the script. Poll numbers are tumbling to historic depths, driven by persistent inflation, rising fuel costs and an increasingly unpopular war in Iran. For the first time since his improbable political resurrection, Trump’s aura of authority is fading.

Rick Wilson, a longtime Republican strategist, prophesied: “This is the beginning of the end. This is the decline. As powerful and transgressive as he’s been, the country does not have a positive outlook right now. In fact, the negativity and pessimism among voters has reached a point that is unparalleled since Jimmy Carter.”

Trump’s self-belief never wavers. He faced four criminal cases and two assassination attempts before winning the 2024 election. He has lived by a mantra of “it will all work out well in the end” while his supporters wear hats that state: “Trump was right about everything.”

Yet he has had a rough month. The Federal Reserve defied him on interest rates. The supreme court blocked his administration’s attempt to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots for November’s midterm elections. One judge prevented him adding his name to the Kennedy Center, prompting him to threaten the national arts complex with demolition; another judge blocked his ban on three news outlets from the White House grounds, ordering the administration to “immediately return, reinstate and restore” their access.

Now even Trump’s dependable power base, the Republican party, is showing cracks amid fears that he will cost them seats in November. In Florida, his home state, gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds quietly scrubbed most Trump references from his campaign website, while the congresswoman María Elvira Salazar ran campaign advertisements openly declaring that federal immigration enforcement had gone “too far” and asserting that Latino voters “feel betrayed”.

Wilson, a co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, sees a herd mentality among congressional Republicans and compares the current mood to a wildlife documentary.

“It needs a David Attenborough voiceover,” he said. “It’s like the gazelles wandering the savannah. They’re sniffing the wind now and they smell something in the wind. They know it’s a predator but they don’t know what to do about it yet. What they haven’t realised is that the predator has been among them all along. The risk factor that they face now is Trump.”

For nearly a decade, elected Republicans maintained a posture of submission, fearful of drawing a primary challenger or a scathing post on Truth Social. But with the elections looming and control of Congress hanging in the balance, self-preservation is rapidly overriding loyalty to the president.

Wilson said: “Now it’s reached the point where the magic doesn’t work any more. There’s no political upside from a president who is at 29% approval rating in some polls, has presided over a disastrous war, and has ended up raising energy prices and food prices – all the things that they can’t spin away.

“The voters now have very much put that together. They associate the war with Trump. They associate the gas prices with Trump. They associate the grocery prices with Trump.”

This creates a vicious circle, Wilson argues. “The more he becomes a liability, the more he acts out. The more he demands loyalty from people and doesn’t get it, the more he demands loyalty from people and doesn’t get it. Everything was handed to him for a decade by that party and, now that they’re paying the price, they’ve decided this has got a little too hairy.”

Faced with shrinking authority and a hostile economic landscape, Trump has reverted to his trusted playbook: manufacturing spectacle, picking cultural fights and raging against the press. His recent decision to ban the news outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House campus following critical coverage was viewed by critics not as a display of strength, but a symptom of deep frustration.

The administration rejects such charges and insists that the president’s agenda is succeeding. Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said in an email: “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.

“The president signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, drove violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution, added more than a million private-sector jobs, and sent Americans’ 401(k)s climbing to record highs,” he added. “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”

But the trend lines are only set to worsen for Trump. If Democrats gain control of the House of Representatives, they plan to launch investigations into how he has allegedly abused his office to enrich his family, grant favours to supporters, hollow out the federal government and carry out expensive construction projects. The attention economy, meanwhile, will inexorably shift to the 2028 presidential race and the question of succession.

Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, said the inevitable shift of focus toward potential candidates – such as the vice-president, JD Vance, or the secretary of state, Marco Rubio – will be cause for friction.

“Nothing will drive him crazier than the shift of the spotlight away from him,” said Galston, a former domestic policy adviser to Bill Clinton. “The prospect of passing the torch, giving up the spotlight, is intensely painful for him. It’s his oxygen. Will he be able to breathe, spiritually and emotionally speaking, without it?”

Trump is not the first president to run into trouble after winning re-election. From Richard Nixon’s Watergate downfall to Clinton’s impeachment and George W Bush’s quagmire in Iraq, second terms have historically served as the graveyard of presidential ambition.

Allan Lichtman, author of a new book, Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation, calls it “the second term curse”. He noted: “Second terms have been remarkably difficult for presidents.”

Lichtman, a history professor at American University in Washington, believes that Trump is driven by two things: money and glory. “He cannot stand not being the centre of attention and that’s dangerous,” he said. “I don’t care much about his verbal lashing-out; I don’t think that helps him at all. But who knows what crazy things he might do to reassert attention on him? And that’s frightening.

“Never underestimate the power of the president. Just because Republicans are criticising him, his poll numbers are low, prospects for Republicans look dim, doesn’t mean he doesn’t have enormous power – and he is certainly quite willing to use that power unconstrained. He doesn’t care about the courts and doesn’t care about the Congress.”

From this perspective, Trump’s last refuge will be the unchecked use of executive authority, a politicised justice department and a sweeping pardon power. With nothing to lose in his final two years, he could go out all guns blazing.

Charlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster, said: “Donald Trump fears irrelevance more than anything and he’ll rage against it as long as he can. The notion that he will go quietly would be incredibly naive.

“We’re headed for a collision between a lame duck who has no respect for the constitutional norms and an opposition that may have some power to hold him accountable. The paradox is the weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets.”

title: Court rules Trump can blacklist Anthropic for refusing to enable Claude features
description: Overly constrained AI models" could cause military operations to fail, judges say.
fullText:
A US appeals court today approved the Department of Defense’s blacklisting of Anthropic technology. Judges decided the Trump administration had authority to blacklist Anthropic for withholding certain AI features from the military even if Anthropic had no malicious intent.

In a 2-1 ruling issued by the US Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit, a panel of judges said the “case raises profoundly difficult questions about the appropriate military uses of an almost unimaginably powerful new technology.” The US “raises the deeply sobering prospect of overly constrained AI models shutting down unexpectedly and thus causing important military operations to fail. Anthropic raises the deeply sobering prospect of unconstrained AI models hallucinating inappropriate targets for lethal military force,” the ruling said.

Trump and Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth “must determine how best to balance the competing risks,” the court said. “In doing so here, the Secretary did not transgress any limits on his authority under the Supply Chain Security Act or the Constitution. Accordingly, we deny the petitions for review.” The same court previously denied Anthropic’s emergency motion for a stay in April.

The two judges who ruled against Anthropic were both appointed by Trump and served in the first Trump administration. Judge Gregory Katsas was previously deputy counsel to the president, and Judge Neomi Rao served in the Trump administration’s Office of Management and Budget.

Anthropic sued the Trump administration in March after it ordered federal agencies to stop using Anthropic’s products and banned defense contractors from doing any business with Anthropic. Anthropic may appeal today’s ruling, either by asking for an en banc review with all of the appeals court judges or by petitioning the Supreme Court.

“We respectfully disagree with the court’s decision,” an Anthropic spokesperson told CNBC. “Another federal court has already held the government’s parallel designation unlawful. We remain confident in our position and are considering all options, including further review.” Despite the ongoing legal battle, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick recently said the Trump administration and Anthropic have patched up their relationship and are “in tune.”

Two courts have been reviewing the US blacklisting of Anthropic. A judge in US District Court for the Northern District of California ruled last month that the action was illegal because Anthropic does not meet the definition of a supply-chain risk, which is limited to “the risk that an adversary may sabotage, maliciously introduce unwanted function, or otherwise subvert… a covered system.”

Today’s ruling from the DC Circuit did not dispute the district court’s primary finding. But it said the district court was tasked with reviewing whether the decision was allowed under one law while the appeals court has exclusive jurisdiction to review the decision under a different, more permissive grant of authority.

The district court decision found a violation of 10 U.S.C. § 3252, in which supply chain risks are limited to malicious actions by adversaries. The appeals court reviewed the blacklisting under 41 U.S.C. § 4713, which doesn’t have the same restrictions. Notably, Congress gave the DC Circuit appeals court exclusive jurisdiction to review procurement actions taken under Section 4713 designations.

We have no quarrel with the Northern District’s conclusion that use of the critical noun adversary, combined with the sinister connotation fairly pervading the string of sabotage, maliciously introduce, and otherwise subvert, indicate that bad motive is required to support a designation under section 3252. Likewise, we have no quarrel with the Northern District’s conclusion that Anthropic has acted with no such bad motive in its dealings with the Department. But as explained at length above, no such bad motive is required to support a designation under the much broader definition set forth in section 4713.

The US designated Anthropic as a supply chain risk under both 3252 and 4713. The latter statute defines “supply chain risk” as “the risk that any person may sabotage, maliciously introduce unwanted function, extract data, or otherwise manipulate the design, integrity, manufacturing, production, distribution, installation, operation, maintenance, disposition, or retirement” of covered technology products “so as to surveil, deny, disrupt, or otherwise manipulate the function, use, or operation of” those products or the information stored or transmitted on them, the court said.

The use of “any person” shows that the definition is not limited to adversaries or foreign entities, the court said. The court also pointed to the word “deny,” which it said applies to Anthropic preventing the US from using certain Claude features.

“In sum, we conclude that the Secretary’s concern about Anthropic disabling Claude from performing lawful actions requested by the Department qualifies as a ‘supply chain risk’ within the meaning of section 4713,” the court majority said. It also said “the Department reasonably feared that Anthropic might manipulate Claude’s design to prevent it from performing national-security functions that the Department deems contractually authorized and necessary.”

The dissenting vote was cast by Judge Karen Henderson, a George H.W. Bush appointee. Henderson disputed the majority’s reading of the definition in 4713, saying that when “viewed in their statutory context, the verbs at issue are all directed at deliberately impeding or eavesdropping on the ‘function, use, or operation’ of a covered article that has entered the federal supply chain.”

Congress “enacted the statute in response to calls from the US intelligence community for legislation to meet the threat of ‘[h]ostile nation state and other bad actors’ infiltrating the federal government’s information and technology systems through its supply chains,” Henderson wrote. She said the definition should not be interpreted to cover “a contractor’s honest and upfront enforcement of restrictions on a covered article’s use disfavored by the government.”

Anthropic alleged, and the district court judge in California agreed, that the Trump administration illegally retaliated against the company after it refused to drop restrictions on the use of its products for lethal autonomous warfare and mass surveillance of Americans.

The appeals court said that Anthropic “encodes restrictions into Claude that prevent the model from performing tasks that Anthropic wishes to prevent. On more than one occasion, these restrictions have stopped Claude from performing tasks requested by government users. And recently, a dispute arose over whether the contractual prohibitions barred the use of Claude in an ongoing overseas military operation, leaving the Department uncertain whether Claude would perform as needed and intended.”

The case in the Northern District of California was presided over by Judge Rita Lin, a Biden appointee. Lin determined that the blacklisting violated the First Amendment. “The empty invocation of national security is not a blank check to punish and retaliate against government critics,” she wrote.

title: Sandbagged: Hoping to steal Nvidia chips, thieves mistakenly grab 20tons of sand
description: Nvidia-branded trailers were too tempting to pass up, but were dumped when the crooks realized what was inside.
fullText:
Nvidia-branded trailers were dumped when the crooks realized what was actually inside.

Whoever stole a pair of trailers plastered with company logos for Nvidia and PlusAI this week in Fremont probably thought they’d scored a fortune in high-tech hardware.

What they actually got was a bunch of sand. About 40,000 pounds of it.

Two trailers belonging to PlusAI — a self-driving trucking company headquartered in Santa Clara — were pilfered late Wednesday from the docks of its Fremont warehouse, police and a company official confirmed.

The trailers held a combined 20 tons of sand, which the company uses to simulate real freight during research and development, according to Jocelyn Ren, a senior marketing manager.

Warehouse workers discovered the theft early Thursday, reporting it to the Fremont Police Department just after 9:30 a.m. The locks on the trailers’ glad hands — the couplings that link the air brakes to the truck — appeared to have been forced off, the company said. The PlusAI cabs that normally pull the test trailers were parked elsewhere on the property and appeared untouched.

Security footage shows two unidentified tractors driving around the warehouse, according to Lauren Kwan, the company’s vice president of marketing. “Those were not our tractors,” she said. “Those were from the thieves.”

The company began filing police and insurance reports. Then, just hours after reporting the theft, a break came from an unlikely source.

PlusAI’s vice president of legal got a text from a friend with a photo of the trailers parked outside an office in Newark — minutes from where they’d been stolen.

“I have been proud of you for your adventure and success at Plus,” the friend wrote. “Just saw two of your trucks near my work place! :)”

PlusAI sent its fleet operations team to confirm that the trailers were still in Newark and alerted the cops. Newark police officers recovered both trailers and returned them to the company.

According to PlusAI, police said it looked like the thieves had broken open the backs of the trailers, found nothing of value, and abandoned them.

Kwan thinks the trailers’ paint job made them a target. One featured joint branding with Nvidia, which has worked with PlusAI to develop self-driving trucks.

“The very apparent branding probably made them think there was very valuable equipment back there,” she said.

No one has been arrested for the theft, and the case remains open, Fremont police said. Newark police didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Kwan said nothing like this has happened in her seven years at PlusAI, which employs about 200 people. The Fremont warehouse is where the company tests its vehicles.

“The whole day was bizarre,” Kwan said.

Michael is a deputy breaking news editor at The Standard.

title: Causal analyst agent skill for Claude
description: Causal analysis for people who aren't data scientists: an Agent Skill for Claude - kiritbasu/causal-analyst
fullText:
Causal analysis for people who aren't data scientists. An Agent Skill that lets Claude answer "did X actually cause Y?" from your data. You bring the question and what you know about your business. Claude does the modelling, checks how far to trust the answer, and hands back a one-page report. When the data can't answer the question, it says so.

Live example reports: Loyalty program (grade C) · Sales calls (grade D, "can't tell") · AI training (grade B, three traps) · Quick start

Contents: Why this exists · What it's like to use · The report · Quick start · How it works · Does it work? · Which model to use · Data and privacy · Limitations and roadmap

Good causal analysis needs two kinds of knowledge that rarely sit in one person:

The marketing lead knows that "points redeemed" only exists after someone joins, and that the program was pushed to big spenders. The data scientist knows that controlling for points will wreck the estimate, and that targeting big spenders creates a gap that isn't the program's doing. Usually it takes both people and a lot of back and forth. Often the domain expert simply ends up with a correlation.

This skill lets the domain expert work directly with Claude. Claude handles the modelling. It asks, in plain language, only the questions that need domain knowledge, turns the answers into a causal diagram the expert confirms, then runs and checks the analysis and explains the result. The expert supplies what only they know; the skill supplies the rest.

It also guards against the ways capable models go wrong. Frontier models already get the arithmetic right: in our tests plain Claude matched the skill's estimate on a clean case to within a few percent. The failures are judgment calls:

So the workflow puts those judgments in the open. Controls are confirmed as recorded before the treatment. The expert signs off the diagram. The method is fixed in advance. There's an explicit "we can't tell" grade, and the risk from hidden factors is sized.

You attach a file and ask in your own words. The skill takes it from there, stopping three times for your input.

You: [attaches customers.csv] Did our loyalty program actually raise monthly spend? We think newer customers benefit more.

1. Claude checks the data and points out anything odd before going further:

4,000 customers, 9 columns. points_redeemed almost perfectly predicts who joined, which usually means it's a result of joining. And 44% of non-members have some points, which shouldn't happen. I'll flag that.

2. It confirms what each column means. Column names mislead (is usage_idx measured before or after the training?), so Claude writes down its reading of every column and when it was recorded, and you correct it.

3. It asks what only you know, one question at a time, as clickable options:

Were income, tenure, age, city and last quarter's spend all recorded before customers joined? ○ Yes ○ Some were later ○ Not sure

Is there anything that affects both who joins and how much they spend that isn't in this file? ○ No ○ Yes: ___ ○ Not sure

Could past spending have driven who joined, rather than only the other way round? ○ Yes, big spenders were targeted ○ No ○ Not sure

4. You confirm the diagram and the plan. Claude draws how it thinks things work, you correct it, and the main method is fixed before anything runs. Where you weren't sure, Claude writes down the alternative diagrams too.

5. You get the report about a minute later. It gives the answer, how much to trust it and why, who benefits most, and the randomized test that would settle it.

A self-contained HTML page: it works offline, on a phone, and prints cleanly. It reads top to bottom as a story. Here is the answer; here is what it stood on; here is how sure we are; here is what to do.

When the data can't answer the question, the report leads with that. The diagram shows why, and the page gives what can be said: a range the true effect lies in, and how to find out.

Open the full reports: loyalty program (grade C) · sales calls (grade D) · AI training (grade B: a misleadingly named mediator, a collider and reverse causation). The HTML files, data and every intermediate file are in examples/.

Claude apps (claude.ai / desktop): download causal-analyst.skill from Releases and upload it in Settings, under Skills. Then attach a data file and ask your question. The skill triggers on questions like "did our loyalty program raise spend?" or "is this cause or just coincidence?"

Claude Code: copy skills/causal-analyst/ into ~/.claude/skills/ (personal) or .claude/skills/ (project).

Python dependencies are installed automatically where the environment allows. Otherwise:

Without an agent: the toolkit is a plain CLI, so you can reproduce any report by hand:

For amount treatments (e.g. discount size), the skill uses g-computation with the outcome model chosen by cross-validation. For "can't tell" cases it reports Manski / Manski–Pepper bounds, or instrument-based bounds and the complier effect when a random nudge exists.

Checks on the diagram itself. A correct method on the wrong diagram gives a confident wrong answer, so the run also tests the design:

Trust grades: A randomized and checks pass · B observational, good overlap, robust to moderate hidden bias · C a weakness (weak overlap, fragile to hidden bias, methods disagree) · D the data can't answer this.

We ran the skill-creator eval loop on three scenarios, comparing Claude with the skill against Claude with the same prompt and no skill (details):

Assertion pass rate: 100% with the skill vs 50–57% without, at about 2–3 minutes and ~20% more tokens per run. Accuracy on clean cases is similar either way; on the AI-training case both runs avoided every trap, which tells us current frontier models handle well-described traps. The skill's added value there is the checks and the audit trail: the report shows what the answer would have been under each wrong diagram. The difference is honest ranges, abstention, pre-registration, and a report someone can act on.

The foundation-model cross-checks were benchmarked on 14 semi-synthetic datasets (results):

CausalPFN was more accurate, especially under poor overlap, but overconfident. That is why the main method stays classical-ML and the foundation models are cross-checks.

The model matters less for the numbers (they're scripted) and more for knowing when not to trust them. That is where we'd spend on the strongest model available.

Contributions, especially eval results on other models and new test cases with known answers, are welcome: see CONTRIBUTING.

Built on DoWhy (identification cross-check), EconML (double ML, causal forests), scikit-learn, statsmodels, and optionally CausalPFN and TabPFN. Methods: Robins, Rotnitzky & Zhao (1994); Chernozhukov et al. (2018); Wager & Athey (2018); Cinelli & Hazlett (2020); Manski (1990); Manski & Pepper (2000); Balazadeh et al. (2025); Hollmann et al. (2025).

title: A Decade of MakeCode
description: Posted on September 25th, 2026 by Jaqster
fullText:
Posted on September 25th, 2026 by Jaqster

This month, we’re celebrating this 10-year milestone to reflect on the impact MakeCode has made, to thank the community and partners who made it possible, and blow out the candles to make wishes for the future!

When MakeCode began, we had a simple idea: everyone should have the opportunity to learn computer science by creating something meaningful.

We wanted to make programming approachable for beginners without making it less powerful for those who were ready to go further. Blocks could provide a welcoming entry point, while JavaScript and Python could give learners a path toward text-based programming.

But we also know that coding is most exciting when you can see your ideas come to life and the end artifact is something you’re proud of sharing.

That’s why MakeCode has always connected programming with things young people love to build and explore - gadgets, games, Minecraft, music, and art.

Over the past decade, that vision has grown into a family of products used in classrooms, libraries, camps, clubs, homes, and maker spaces around the world.

Learn more about MakeCode at makecode.com

The mission of Microsoft MakeCode is to inspire new generations of technology creators. We are incredibly proud of the impact MakeCode has had on the lives of young people around the world.

Over 100 million students have used and hopefully been inspired by MakeCode since it launched. And it’s had a truly global impact – used in 37 different languages and over 156 different countries, and in 51 of those countries over 10,000 students are using MakeCode regularly every month. Just yesterday, students spent 128,175 hours combined working on their MakeCode projects – that’s over 350 years of learning in a single day! And in a month, 70,239,275 blocks or lines of code are created in MakeCode by students – for comparison, the Linux operating system is 42M lines of code!

A milestone like this isn’t really about a product though… it’s about people.

It’s about the teacher who spends the extra time prepping for a physical computing activity to engage a student who never thought coding was for them.

Elizabeth Bacon is a middle school computer science teacher at Wildwood School in Los Angeles who is using MakeCode Arcade in a “Build a game for a friend” project to strengthen user-centered design skills and practice collaboration and empathy in the classroom. She is also using MakeCode for micro:bit in the class’s capstone project of a mini-golf Putt-Putt Course. We met with her class last week to learn more about the student projects.

Ms. Bacon’s 6th grade class joining with the MakeCode Team

Stu Lowe is the Learning Technology Specialist at Beacon Hill Elementary School in Hong Kong and a longtime MakeCode user. Here’s a short video he put together on why he uses MakeCode in the classroom.

It’s about the student who spends an afternoon debugging a function until it finally works.

Prabhath is an 11-year-old who has spent time creating MakeCode games and learning on his own. We got the chance to meet this young man recently and were inspired by his passion and motivation for game development! He also gave us some really good product feedback and ideas for new features.

Prabhath’s MakeCode experiences

It’s about the parent who drives their child every week to a Code Ninjas center.

It’s about the librarian, camp counselor, volunteer, and instructor who creates a space where young people can experiment and ask, “What happens if I try this?”

It’s about incredible partners who have helped shaped and expanded what’s possible with MakeCode.

A huge heartfelt ❤️ Thank You ❤️ to all of our Partners – especially the Micro:bit Educational Foundation and the Minecraft Education Team. We would not be here without you. But also to Adafruit, the Blockly Team, Calliope, Chibitronics, Code Ninjas, ElecFreaks, Forward Education, GitHub, Kitronik, Kittenbot, Lancaster University, Makey Makey and many more! Thank you all for taking a bet on us!

And, finally, it’s about the incredible community members who translate, share projects, answer questions, submit issues and PR’s, contribute ideas, create extensions, and help others get started.

Here’s a story from one of our MakeCode Forum members –

The first time I used MakeCode was through the Project Lead The Way program in elementary school. We played with Micro:bits. It was a short, maybe one week activity. Then, in middle school, one of my friends introduced me to Makecode Arcade, and I have been making games ever since.

I joined the MakeCode forum when I was 13 and posted very little for 2 years. Then, one day, I started helping people solve their bugs… and it was super fun! Helping others with their code is one of my favorite things to do on the forum now. The puzzle of finding the error, and the satisfaction of fixing it, are what have kept me solving bugs on this forum for so long, not to mention the amazing community, devs, and MakeCode Arcade itself!

The other thing I learned while using MakeCode was JavaScript. Writing code in blocks, switching to the JavaScript editor, and looking at what the block code turned into was a big step in learning JavaScript and written code in general. Reading the JavaScript code running behind each block helped me better solve peoples’ block code issues too, and now I also make extensions!

Now I’m in college majoring in Computer Science, and I owe it all to MakeCode Arcade.

To everyone who has taught with MakeCode, learned with MakeCode, built with MakeCode, contributed to MakeCode, or simply encouraged someone else to give coding a try: Thank you. We are so grateful for your trust in this product and for your help in inspiring the next generation of technology creators.

The world of technology has changed dramatically since MakeCode launched. Artificial intelligence is transforming how we interact with computers and build things. The need has never been greater for people of all backgrounds and perspectives to understand computational thinking and to be able to use technology creatively to help us shape the future together.

We want to continue making computer science fun and accessible to more learners, supporting educators with high-quality classroom experiences, and giving students opportunities to explore AI and emerging technologies through hands-on creation while preserving the process of learning and discovery.

We’re excited about where MakeCode can go next, and especially about what you will build with it!

Please share your birthday wishes for MakeCode here: https://www.kudoboard.com/boards/KxJ5V6Cp

description:

fullText:
New research suggests the technology could be used to increase out-of-hospital access to life-saving devices

Drones could help cut the time it takes to get a defibrillator to people experiencing cardiac arrests when not in hospital, researchers have suggested.

In the UK alone, there are more than 30,000 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests a year where emergency medical services attempt to resuscitate the individual, according to the British Heart Foundation. However, fewer than one in 10 people survive such an event, and some who do are left with neurological problems.

One important factor that can affect survival is how rapidly victims get access to treatment – every minute without CPR and defibrillation reduces the chance of survival by 10%.

“We have an objective as EMS [emergency medical service] organisations and EMS physicians to help cardiac arrest patients get defibrillated as early as possible,” said Matthieu Heidet, a professor of emergency medicine at Henri-Mondor university hospital in Créteil, France.

Work by Heidet and colleagues has suggested drones could be used to increase access to the life-saving devices.

To explore the issue, the team analysed the number and location of 28,349 out-of-hospital cardiac arrests that occurred between 2011 and 2024 in administrative areas within the Greater Paris area. Central Paris was excluded from the analysis.

The team cross-referenced these events with the location of fixed automated external defibrillators (AEDs).

The researchers found accessibility of the 1,893 AEDs varied considerably across the area.

“Only 30% of all [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] cases occurred within the target 500-metre network distance of the nearest recorded fixed AED,” said Dr Hillary Minka, an emergency physician at the Lariboisière hospital in Paris and the first author of the work.

The team found an extra 910 fixed AEDs would be needed for 84.5% of the recorded cardiac arrest cases to have been within 500 metres of an AED, while 1,712 extra fixed AEDs would be needed for 100% coverage.

However, by using drones operating within a radius of 3,900 metres, coverage could be increased with fewer devices.

“As drone bases were introduced, the number of additional fixed AEDs required fell substantially,” said Minka, noting that with 100 drone bases and 26 additional fixed AEDs, more than 97% of the cardiac arrest cases would have been located either within 500 metres of a fixed AED or within approximately 4km (2.5 miles) of a drone base. The use of 200 drone bases and just four extra AEDs meant more than 99% of cases would have been covered.

The researchers also looked at the proportion of the cardiac arrest cases deemed close enough to an existing fixed AED that the device could be retrieved in a round trip within five minutes.

The results revealed only 30-40% of the cardiac arrest cases had access to current fixed AEDs within this time period using the ground transportation network.

Heidet added that this figure was optimistic. “In France, only 8% of out-of-hospital cardiac arrest patients benefit from the application of a public AED before the arrival of the [emergency services],” he said, noting one factor is that a large proportion of AEDs are inaccessible, for example because they are housed in enclosed private spaces that are not open at all times.

The team’s models were based on drones being housed at sites ranging from current AED locations to fire stations and mobile intensive care units, and did not look at real-world deployment of such tech.

Heidet noted it is not the first time drones have been considered for the delivery of AEDs; the approach is already being used in parts of Sweden and has saved lives.

In real-world systems, Heidet added, drones are operated by trained drone pilots.

“Once an emergency call is received and an [out-of-hospital cardiac arrest] is identified at the dispatch centre, the drone is activated by EMS dispatchers. It then takes off and follows an automated flight path, while the final approach and subsequent AED delivery are handled by the drone pilot. The entire process is conducted under the supervision of the emergency medical service,” he said. Once delivered, the AED can be used by members of the public at the scene.

Heidet added the cost of drones needed to be integrated into the evaluation of such technology, noting there may be a balance between the ideal model and the feasible economic model.

The study, which has not yet been peer-reviewed, is to be presented at the European Emergency Medicine Congress in Paris on Saturday.

title: Bellamy support crucial after serious injury - Wales' Burns
description: Winger Wes Burns hopes to repay Craig Bellamy's support during a long-term injury by making an impact for Wales in the Nations League.
fullText:
It is usually the manager who pulls a player to one side before or after training to offer a word of advice or appreciation.

But it was the other way round with Craig Bellamy and Wes Burns.

Wales winger Burns says he made a point of pulling Bellamy aside to thank him for the "massive" support he gave him after a career-threatening knee injury that ended his Premier League dream in 2025.

Without Bellamy's backing, Burns said, his Wales career might have gone the same way.

"The world of football forgets you very, very fast when you're not playing," said the 31-year-old, who's back with the national team for the first time in two years.

"But when someone of Craig Bellamy's stature, the head coach of Wales, is calling me every month, or once every two weeks, to make sure I'm doing well... it's a massive, massive plus.

"Rather than feeling a million miles away, it always made me feel I was in touching distance of getting back in."

You can understand why Burns initially feared the worst.

He was out for almost a year after suffering a torn anterior cruciate ligament during Ipswich Town's defeat at Liverpool in January 2025.

The Cardiff-born winger was never completely off Bellamy's mind, though, and now he wants to make up for lost international minutes by playing a part in the Nations League campaign that began with Thursday's 1-0 defeat in Portugal.

Sunday, 27 September, 17:00 BST

Live on BBC iPlayer, BBC One Wales, BBC Sounds, BBC Radio Wales, Radio Cymru and 5 Live, BBC Sport website and app, plus live text commentary.

Burns did not make it off the subs' bench in Lisbon, but hopes to get some minutes in Wales' second Nations League tie against Denmark in Copenhagen on Sunday, 27 October.

After the injury trauma that cut short his fairytale journey from League One to the Premier League with Ipswich, though, he is just pleased to be back on the international scene at all.

"You just have to remember you're only one second away from disaster, really," said Burns.

"That's how I felt when the injury happened. You feel that could be the end of your career because you never know how bad the injury is initially.

"And when you've had surgery, and your knee's like a balloon, you're thinking 'how on earth am I even going to walk again, never mind play'.

"Everything heals in time, though, and it was just about making sure I got the rehab right. The phone calls from Craig, knowing he had a similar injury when he was younger as a player, meant so much to me."

Burns could have been playing Premier League football again this season, having helped Ipswich bounce straight back to the top flight in the 2025-26 campaign.

But the former Fleetwood winger chose instead to drop two divisions to join Leicester City, who have struggled to adapt to life in League One under former Swansea City boss Russell Martin.

"I could've done another year at Ipswich, and I was weighing up whether to finish the story of playing a full season in the Premier League (which injury deprived him of the previous time) - a level I'd worked so hard to get back to," said Burns.

"But I also had to think about the longevity of my career, and in the end I took the option of a longer contract at Leicester and possibly recreating what I'd already done at Ipswich (back-to-back promotions)."

Such a journey might seem remote right now, with Leicester sitting 13th in League One with just two wins from their opening seven games, but Burns insists the Foxes will improve as the season goes on.

"We all know the story - Leicester, Premier League champions 10 years ago, amazing Champions League run, FA Cup winners and now sort of sitting mid-table in League One," he said.

"But it feels like they're very much in the same spot as when I went into Ipswich.

"It's a chance to recreate something that I've done in the past with an amazing manager (Martin) who obviously gets a lot of stick.

"He has a style of play and a philosophy that's very, very football-based and high risk but when that works it's amazing.

"Trust me - I've played against very good Russell Martin teams and they're very hard to play against, but it's a process and processes take a long time.

"I've got no doubt it's going to pick up, for sure."

Burns' last outing for Leicester was a 30-minute cameo off the bench at Barnsley on 19 September.

One week on, he hopes to step back onto the international stage for the first time since starting Wales' 1-0 win over Montenegro in Nations League B in October 2024.

From Oakwell in Barnsley to Copenhagen in Denmark, followed by a Cardiff City Stadium meeting with Erling Haaland's Norway on Thursday, 1 October.

"Going from the weekly level of football I'm now at to possibly playing against Norway, Denmark or Portugal (at home next month)... obviously the gap in quality is going to be massive," said Burns.

"But I've had experience of playing in the Premier League and against very good international teams.

"The one that stands out for me is when we played Netherlands away in the Nations League (in 2022), and I was on the same pitch as (midfielder) Frenkie de Jong - still to this day the best player I've ever played against or witnessed on a football field.

"So just drawing on experiences like that, and big games I've played in, will definitely help if I do get on the pitch against Denmark and Norway.

"It's just so exciting to be involved in games like these."

Bellamy wants more from Wales after loss to Portugal

Felix strike earns Portugal narrow win over Wales

title: Charles brothers 'brilliant' in NI's landmark win
description: The Charles brothers led the way for Northern Ireland at both ends of the field during the side's Nations League win over Georgia in Tbilisi.
fullText:
It seems even when sibling rivalry reaches the level of international football, older brothers still make a habit of stealing the show.

As the clock ticked beyond 97 minutes in Northern Ireland's Nations League B Group 2 opener against Georgia in Tbilisi on Friday, goalkeeper Pierce Charles seemed sure to be the man making the headlines.

Quite apart from saving a penalty from Ballon d'Or nominee Khvicha Kvaratskhelia in the second half, the Queens Park Rangers loanee had made a handful of other smart stops to preserve what was set to be Northern Ireland's first competitive clean sheet away from home since Charles' 2024 international debut against Belarus.

A credible point on the road would have represented a solid start to the campaign for Michael O'Neill's side on their return to the second tier of the competition after six years away, especially after Georgia had significantly upped the tempo after the break.

But then, in the 99th minute, up popped the more senior Charles sibling, Shea, with Northern Ireland's latest ever goal, to give the 60 or so visiting fans the most memorable of away days.

"Classic Shea," laughed Pierce when asked whether his brother had stolen his thunder.

In truth, this was a night in Tbilisi when both brothers deserved a sizeable share of the credit for leading the side to a first ever away win in the Nations League.

Northern Ireland manager O'Neill said: "The two boys were brilliant. I thought Pierce played extremely well, not just his distribution but he makes a big save in the second half as well.

"He gives you a great range of control because of his passing and everything around that. He gives the back three a lot of security because they know they can go back there.

"Shea was colossal, not just on the ball but I felt physically, his ability to step past people, the amount of time he was fouled and the referee for some reason didn't want to produce a card despite the number of fouls on him. I thought he was fabulous."

On what Pierce, 21, felt was his best performance in a Northern Ireland shirt, it was the goalkeeper rather than the match-winner who picked up player-of-the-match honours.

While he credited pre-match research for his denial of Paris St-Germain star Kvaratskhelia from 12 yards, his older brother always believed he had the big moment in him.

"I always back Pierce. He's done really well to save it and make a few other a really good saves. It's credit to him for the win," Shea said.

"I thought after the penalty save we really stuck together and got a bit of control of the game. I think that's why we've come away with the win."

NI win in Georgia after Kvaratskhelia penalty miss

O'Neill left 'baffled' by refereeing in late win

The Fulham midfielder felt he should have scored "a couple more" before his late strike, but this was another commanding performance in the middle of the park from the 22-year-old.

More and more used to the big stage, he has already faced Liverpool, Manchester United and Chelsea since his summer switch from Southampton to Craven Cottage.

The Manchester City youth product believes coming up against the likes of Rodri, Sandro Tonali and Christian Eriksen during his international career has eased his transition into the top flight.

"It's helped me a lot," Shea said.

"I remember when we played the Spain game [in June 2024], I said these are the kind of people you play against in the Premier League, so it's all experience.

"I feel really good and I think our team as well is in a really good place. Everyone's getting a lot of minutes at club level so when we're coming here we're only getting stronger every time."

There will be little rest for the group as, after flying home in the early hours of Saturday morning, they face Hungary at Windsor Park on Monday night in what is the second fixture of this four-game window.

A first game in Belfast since November, and one that will be shown live across the BBC, the older Charles brother is keen to harness the momentum of a rare away win when returning to home soil.

"I think it just sets us up really well for the Hungary game on Monday. This is really exciting and hopefully we can push on," Shea added.

"Everyone's buzzing and can't wait to get back to Belfast and just try and get the win there."
