title: MTV used to rule pop culture. Now it mostly breaks through once a year.
description:
MTV, the 45-year-old network and music video pioneer, was once the arbiter of cool. They played all the hottest new songs from some of the biggest stars the country has ever seen: Madonna, David Bowie, Michael Jackson and Prince. They ushered in the era of boy band domination and made a space for teen culture to thrive. 
Now, MTV isn't dead, but it's more of a nostalgic icon than a network that people turn on to actively watch or listen to music. These days, you'll find seemingly endless reruns of the 49-season clip show Ridiculousness, which stopped making new episodes in 2025.
fullText:
MTV, the 45-year-old network and music video pioneer, was once the arbiter of cool. They played all the hottest new songs from some of the biggest stars the country has ever seen: Madonna, David Bowie, Michael Jackson and Prince. They ushered in the era of boy band domination and made a space for teen culture to thrive.

Now, MTV isn't dead, but it's more of a nostalgic icon than a network that people turn on to actively watch or listen to music. These days, you'll find seemingly endless reruns of the 49-season clip show Ridiculousness, which stopped making new episodes in 2025.

Gen X-ers and millennials remember MTV's former life fondly: They recall rushing home from school to catch Total Request Live. But somewhere between "Thriller" and Jersey Shore, the cable channel shifted its identity away from music entirely — save for one night a year, when they air the Video Music Awards. So what happened?

Here's Ridiculousness/MTV schedule for the week of 12/06/2020!

Highlights:
The Challenge: Double Agents premieres Wed @ 8p, with special episode airing on Monday at the same time#MTVSchedule2020 #week50 pic.twitter.com/fFRLgvYkLR

— MTV Schedule (@MTVSchedule) December 8, 2020

To figure out where the network has gone, we have to look back on what it originally was. From the 1980s to the early 1990s, MTV was at its most culturally influential. It launched in 1981, manufactured to captivate teenagers — an audience advertisers weren't reaching well.

Then, VJs, or video jockeys, introduced music videos to audiences of millions. Getting your video to play on the network was an honor.

In the book I Want My MTV: The Uncensored Story of the Music Video Revolution, authors Craig Marks and Rob Tannenbaum explain that making music videos was once an expensive promotional afterthought; MTV, however, made it one of the most important factors in the industry. A video could make or break a career.

"MTV changed the architecture of being an artist," Mark Mothersbaugh of Devo, whose racy video for "Whip It" dominated the network in its early days, says in the book. (In a true sign of the times, Mothersbaugh collaborated on the theme song for Ridiculousness, which is a cover of Devo's "Uncontrollable Urge.")

It was a massive force of monoculture, uniting audiences around the same songs — something nearly unfathomable now that the algorithms powering streaming services tailor what we listen to to our precise tastes.

The reality of differing tastes was a problem MTV quickly encountered. Executives realized that if fans don't like what's playing, they'll change the channel. That means they might not come back, and their value to advertisers could be lost. They started testing different programming, including the 1987 game show Remote Control, but what really hit was 1992's The Real World. The show, which filmed a group of strangers living together, laid the groundwork for modern reality TV.

1993's raunchy animated series Beavis and Butt-Head and 2006's soapy reality program The Hills (a spinoff of the buzzy high school drama Laguna Beach) followed, and MTV became known for more than just music. People said they missed the videos, but did they really, since they were tuning in now more than ever? MTV's most popular show came in 2009 with Jersey Shore, the raucous reality show about hard-partying pals, which ran for six seasons. Its most-watched VMAs were in 2011.

In 2010, MTV dropped the words "Music Television" from the bottom of its iconic logo, signaling that it had entered a new era. Music videos were relegated to spinoff cable channels like MTV Music, MTV 80s, MTV 90s, Club MTV and MTV Live. YouTube had emerged as an on-demand music video streaming platform, so there was no need to endure all the friction of waiting to see an artist you like appear on your television.

With cord-cutting and the rise of streaming services, MTV just couldn't hang, slowly cutting its shows and losing its hold in the youth-driven reality programming space. Parent company Paramount Skydance shut down MTV's U.K. music-only channels at the end of 2025, and rumors began to spread that the network was entirely dead. It's not! We still have reruns of Ridiculousness, and of course, the 2026 VMAs.

"Nobody is saying MTV is what it was when you were 15. But it is still on the air, it is still profitable," former VJ Dave Holmes wrote in Esquire earlier this year.

And the VMAs are still culturally relevant. The 2025 show was its most-watched since 2019 — but that's also because it was simulcast on fellow Paramount network CBS for the first time. Even so, it's an indication that people still want to know what the kids are into musically these days. The nominations for this year's awards suggest MTV would like us to think that's Madonna, but also newer names like Sienna Spiro, Olivia Dean and (of course) Ella Langley.

MTV still programs some music video channels in the U.S., including "MTV Classic" (which plays music videos from the 1980s to 2000s), "MTV Live" (which runs current music videos) and a collection of MTV-branded FAST channels streaming on Pluto like "MTV Biggest Pop," "MTV Spankin' New," "Yo! MTV" and "MTV Flow Latino."

But MTV, or any other TV network, likely won't be able to run on music alone. According to MIDiA Research, 16- to 24-year-olds discover music mostly through TikTok, then YouTube. You can also replicate the MTV VJ experience in your own home by hosting "Gay Guy Music Video Night," a queer party pregame phenomenon in which a friend group queues up pop videos to watch and talk over before heading out. When people get nostalgic about the MTV they grew up with, it's not because they're mourning a steady stream of music videos. It's not the Music Television that people miss, but the way things used to be, when culture was united.

Video may have killed the radio star — which, by the way, was both the first and last music video played on MTV proper — but algorithms killed the video star.

title: The teething troubles with Man Utd's tactics under Olid
description: Eva Olid promised high-possession attacking football at Manchester United, so why has it not worked yet?
fullText:
Eva Olid was given the Manchester United job with a reputation for playing high-possession attacking football and her impressive spell at Hearts demonstrated those ideals.

In her opening weeks in the Women's Super League, however, she has struggled to get her team playing this type of dominant football, even if an eye-catching 10-1 win at Sheffield United in the League Cup on Wednesday suggested she was making progress.

On the WSL's opening night, United lost 2-1 to London City Lionesses before suffering a 5-0 defeat by Chelsea. They responded by drawing 1-1 with Arsenal in a performance far more pragmatic than many might have expected.

Following the turbulent start, we analysed Olid's United, unpacking her tactical approach and the tweaks she has made from predecessor Marc Skinner.

Man Utd put 10 past Blades as Olid gets first win

Olid's Man Utd take big step forward after 'intense week'

Under Olid, United look to play out from the back. For a team ultimately wanting to dominate the ball, short passes help reduce the 50-50 nature of long balls.

Their build-up normally starts from a 4-2 or 3-2 base, with the central midfielders forming a narrow two.

The winger on the same side as the ball tends to stay high and wide, while the far-side winger drops deeper, playing alongside the number 10 and creating a box in midfield.

Although Skinner's United also used a 4-2 or 3-2 base, their principles were different.

His formation was generally a more stretched and symmetrical 3-2-2-3 with players given more fixed positions to occupy.

His number 10s were often asked to stay high in pockets, to either receive the ball in dangerous areas or drag opponents away to create space elsewhere.

Her central players are given greater licence to come towards the ball, likely to create overloads in the middle of the pitch.

For example, if Park switches from the flank into central midfield, should the opposition full-back follow her? If they do not, it should hand United a numerical advantage around the ball.

This reflects in where United now focus their play.

That is because when opponents defend zonally, crowding central areas gives United more numbers in the middle. If defences compensate by narrowing, space appears on the outside for unmarked players.

As with all systems, there are trade-offs.

Skinner's more fixed structure could make it easier for brave opponents to match them player-for-player. In that situation, Olid's team would respond by moving another player towards the ball to create an overload.

Alternatively, by focusing on small-space combinations through the centre, Olid's United are more likely to lose possession in dangerous areas, making them more susceptible to counter-attacks, something that has been evident already in her tenure.

After three league games, United have averaged 37% possession, with Olid identifying two problems last weekend: "We lose simple passes and we cannot recognise the free player."

Goalkeeper Phallon Tullis-Joyce has struggled with the ball at her feet, lacking some of the qualities this system asks for. Chelsea's man-to-man pressure exposed that and prevented United from establishing prolonged possession.

She is not the only one making a tough adjustment to this more intricate approach.

Olid's tactics are designed to create numerical advantages to put players in space but United have not always found them even when the movement has been good.

Her style requires players to be better technically and quicker cognitively.

Playing through crowded central areas means receiving the ball under pressure, combining in small spaces and identifying the spare player. Those actions rely on chemistry and game understanding rather than simply following a pre-planned pattern.

Hinata Miyazawa and Julia Zigiotti-Olme have looked the best suited but developing the collective understanding and removing hesitation will take time.

For Chelsea's fourth goal, these trade-offs were seen clearly as United lost possession trying to play through the middle from deep and were punished in transition.

To her credit, Olid has adapted her approach.

There is recent evidence of Tullis-Joyce going long more often and against Arsenal, recalled Awujo provided a more capable target for those passes than Ella Toone.

This also allowed striker Elisabeth Terland to stay higher up the pitch rather than constantly dropping deep to engage in aerial duels or hold-up play.

She has also explained her approach when out of possession, telling Sky Sports: "We are a team who need to press high."

Against Chelsea, however, that press was repeatedly exposed.

With Monica Jusu Bah starting on the left and Terland leading the press, the former moved inside as the ball travelled wide to try to engage Chelsea midfielder Keira Walsh.

That allowed Blues right-back Ellie Carpenter freedom to advance, while on the other side Wieke Kaptein pinned back United left-back Andrea Medina.

In the second half, Olid adjusted. Terland became more passive alongside Toone, with the pair screening Chelsea's central midfielders.

That allowed Jusu Bah to stay wider and prevent easy access to Carpenter.

In the big win against Sheffield United on Wednesday, Manchester United's third and fourth goal came from an intense and co-ordinated press that forced the opposition to turn over the ball close to their own goal.

Implementing a new style takes time, particularly when players are being asked to use space and accept risk in ways they are not accustomed to.

A common problem for coaches with an ambitious game model is becoming too attached to the final version of it and ignoring what the current squad needs.

Olid does not appear to be falling into that trap.

"The focus [against Arsenal] was the defensive shape," she said. "It's trying to get them more confidence."

Attacking football in this more fluid manner may be the final goal but Olid appears willing to build towards it in steps.

Early on in her managerial role at Hearts, she showed similar flexibility, which won her points, the trust of her players, and a platform from which to create exciting football.

"The [attack] will come," Olid has said. "But we need to keep this [defensive structure], then from there, little by little, be an attacking team, create chances, score more goals."

And the League Cup victory did give some indication it has, although Sheffield United are bottom of WSL 2 in the early weeks of the season.

What will be key is to see how they build on that momentum for this weekend's WSL match against West Ham on Sunday.

title: The boxer who accidentally became an actor
description: Euphoria star Javon Walton discusses his boxing roots, acting career and Saturday's fight with UFC great Henry Cejudo.
fullText:
Javon Walton has spent much of his life performing under bright lights. Sometimes there is a camera in front of him. At other times, there is an opponent trying to punch him back.

To millions, the 20-year-old is better known as Ashtray - the tattooed teenage drug dealer in hit HBO TV drama Euphoria.

But on Saturday, American Walton headlines a Misfits Boxing event in Miami against former two-weight UFC champion and Olympic wrestling gold medallist Henry Cejudo.

You could be forgiven for thinking this is another celebrity trying his hand at boxing in an era of influencer fights and crossover events. But Walton had "zero interest in acting" as a young child - boxing was his first love.

"My parents were boxing fans and when it was on HBO on Saturdays, I would watch it with them," he tells BBC Sport.

"I practically begged my dad to take me to a gym and when I was four years old he finally took me."

Walton has since amassed 85 amateur bouts, twice won silver at the Junior Olympics and is unbeaten as a professional with three wins and a draw. He is signed to Jake Paul and Nakisa Bidarian's Most Valuable Promotions.

Walton competed at a high level in gymnastics after following his sister into the sport, but boxing remained his obsession.

It was the sweet science, somewhat ironically, which eventually opened the door to a completely different form of performance.

Walton appeared on Steve Harvey's television show aged 11 to showcase his boxing ability, throwing combinations on the pads before also demonstrating his gymnastics skills with a backflip.

Casting director Jennifer Venditti saw the appearance and contacted his family about auditioning for Euphoria.

"I was like, 'OK, why not?'" Walton says. "And that just led to one opportunity after another."

What started by accident grew into a substantial acting career. Walton went on to appear in Amazon drama Utopia and Netflix series The Umbrella Academy, and even found himself working alongside the man behind cinema's most famous boxer Rocky Balboa, Sylvester Stallone, in Samaritan.

"I found my love in that space," Walton says. "I look at that as an outlet where I can tap into my emotions because you can't do that in boxing."

The harder challenge now is finding room for both careers. Walton says filming can take him away for six months, while preparing to fight demands an eight-week camp and complete focus.

"My goal is to see how well I can balance both but that's easier said than done," he says. "I kind of have to pick one to focus on."

For now, that focus is Cejudo. The 39-year-old won Olympic freestyle wrestling gold in 2008 before becoming a UFC champion in two weight divisions, but Saturday will be his professional boxing debut.

The bout, which Walton accepted at less than two weeks' notice after Cejudo's original opponent withdrew, has been sanctioned by the Florida State Commission and will count towards their professional records.

"You have to have a level of respect," Walton says. "But at the same time he's stepping into unmarked territory - my field and something I've done my whole life.

"On the mat it would be a different story, but this is the ring."

In Walton's corner will be the man who first took him to a gym as a four-year-old - his father and trainer, DJ.

"What was beautiful about our journey was we got to grow together," Walton says.

"While I was learning how to be a fighter at a young age, he was learning the coaching side. The way I look at it is we're the pilot and co-pilot. He's a head coach who happens to be my dad. I want to do right by us and not just for me."

title: Ward appointed Liverpool's sporting director
description: Julian Ward becomes Liverpool's sporting director for the second time following the departure of Richard Hughes.
fullText:
Liverpool have appointed Julian Ward as the club's new sporting director.

Ward, 45, replaces Richard Hughes, who held the role for just over two years before leaving in September.

This will be Ward's second stint as sporting director at Anfield, having first done the job during the 2022-23 season. He said he was "incredibly excited" to take on the role.

Ward joined Liverpool in 2012 as European scouting manager for Spain and Portugal and was promoted to assistant sporting director in 2020.

He succeeded Michael Edwards two years later but by November 2022, it had been confirmed that Ward would leave at the end of that season.

Ward was brought back in 2024 as Fenway Sports Group's technical director when Liverpool's owners made Edwards their chief executive of football - and has been responsible for overseeing player development pathways and the academy for the past two years.

FSG president Mike Gordon said: "We are delighted that Julian has agreed to take over leadership of our football operations department at this juncture, primarily because it is a role for which we believe he is the ideal candidate given his extensive experience of the football industry in general and Liverpool Football Club in particular.

"The knowledge and expertise he brings will only enhance our football operations, while also ensuring Andoni Iraola is provided with the support he requires as he continues to make such a positive impression as head coach."

Julian Ward's appointment gives Liverpool's hierarchy some much-needed stability after a summer of transition.

Ward has done the sporting director job before - and bar a spell between the summers of 2023 and 2024, has been at the club since 2012.

Liverpool did speak to external candidates but Ward was seen as the stand-out choice.

One source described him as: "Calm, well-spoken and with a clear opinion and vision."

Ward's previous spell as sporting director came under Jurgen Klopp, where he oversaw the signings of Luis Diaz, Cody Gakpo, Alexis Mac Allister and Darwin Nunez - he has a global contacts network and plenty of experience when it comes to negotiations.

He was also influential when Mohamed Salah renewed his contract in 2022 - flying to see Salah on holiday to seal the deal - and his relationship with the agent Jorge Mendes helped Liverpool in their pursuit of Diogo Jota.

There will be plenty of jobs for Ward to tackle - including the securing of Rio Ngumoha on a long-term deal now that he is 18 and determining whether new contracts are offered to Alisson and Virgil van Dijk before their current agreements expire this summer.

As FSG's technical director, Ward played a role in Liverpool's push to recruit younger talent. And he has a good relationship with Mike Gordon, who oversees the day-to-day running of the club.

Under Klopp, Ward left 12 months into a three-year deal, but should have more of a say now, given how the head coach role has been structured under both Arne Slot and his successor Andoni Iraola.

Time will tell if Ward's appointment proves successful - but in the here and now, he looks a more-than-sensible choice.

title: Pocognoli may require patience to deliver on Scotland shake-up
description: A new era begins for Scotland, with Sebastien Pocognoli leading a refreshed squad into the Nations League campaign.
fullText:
The Tartan Army are marching into the unknown as Scotland begin life without Steve Clarke, the nation's longest serving and most successful manager.

For seven years, they were guided by Clarke, who - despite leaving many feeling fatigued by his style of football - led them from the international wilderness to three major tournaments.

Sebastien Pocognoli is the man tasked with filling those big shoes.

The Belgian has already pocketed early goodwill by freshening up the squad, but that cordiality will only carry the 39-year-old so far if the promised style and substance is not delivered.

For co-hosts Scotland, it's harder not to qualify for Euro 2028 than it is to claim one of the 24 places, so that should provide patience for the new boss and the Scottish FA, which has taken a bit of a gamble going loco for Poco.

Scotland will 'learn on the job' under Pocognoli - Robertson

You are the new Scotland boss - what would you do?

New-look squad, but how will Pocognoli's Scotland line-up?

Clarke's reign was more about functionality than flare. It was a formula that brought positive qualifying results, whether fans found it easy on the eye or not.

Some of those colouring the streets of Ljubljana are still scarred from the summer heartache at the prompt World Cup exit, while others are taking notes of the picturesque surroundings as inspiration for statues of the former manager.

Pragmatism hauled Scotland back on to the biggest stage after a 28-year absence.

But, once there, Clarke's side made a pitiful attempt to steal any headlines from the supporters who shone in Boston and Miami.

That's something that will be expected of Pocognoli, making a bit of noise at major tournaments, by way of the nice football he teased, too.

As he acknowledged, the "foundations" are there. Wise old heads remain in the squad and will be required as the young guns make the jump.

Captain Andy Robertson has been impressed by the new additions' "energy and enthusiasm". It's reignited something inside him too.

As long as Pocognoli has the buy-in of the skipper - who he met for dinner and had multiple chats with before kicking off the training camp in La Manga - the rest should follow. And he will need them all.

In Spain, where the squad sweated through their drills earlier this week, players had to be peeled off the pitch, exerting themselves to their fullest in an attempt to put themselves in the frame for a start.

There's a feeling that, although this is a new-look squad, it won't be so much a new-look team. It's more how they're asked to play.

The sweeping assumption is Pocognoli will go with a 3-4-3 - aggressive from the off, suffocating in the final third - in one of the system's many variations.

Several national teams have changed managers since the World Cup, although Pocognoli is not garnering the same attention as Jurgen Klopp, Xavi Hernandez or Zinedine Zidane. Wonder why?

He has overseen just 107 games in his spells in charge at Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco, after a playing career at left-back earned him 13 caps for Belgium.

Compared to Clarke, and many others on the international scene, he is somewhat inexperienced.

As is his squad. Twelve of them were not in the United States. Eight are yearning for a first cap. Pocognoli has cast his first net far and wide.

Sevilla striker Robbie Ure, Brondby captain Luis Binks and late addition Kristi Montgomery may never have had a look in under Clarke. Not an age thing, but Oli McBurnie is finally back with a point to prove.

James Wilson and Findlay Curtis were both capped by Clarke - the latter made two World Cup cameos - but both have been released to the under-21s for their important hosting of Azerbaijan on Wednesday.

The focus on youth, led by SFA chief football officer Craig Mulholland, is a far cry from the output the last time Scotland were in Slovenia.

After an agonising 2-2 draw in 2017, which ended their hopes of a place at the 2018 World Cup, then-manager Gordon Strachan famously pointed towards genetics for his side's failure.

The Slovenes, who appointed former centre-back Bostjan Cesar, sent off in the dying minutes of that game in 2017 back in January, are in a sticky spot with just one win in 10.

Whisper it, but Scotland should win here. But it's about more than that as they get to grips with Pocognoli.

It could be argued there was no better time to roll the dice. It's a relatively stress-free opening for him with Switzerland at home and North Macedonia away before they meet Slovenia again at Hampden on 6 October - all in the knowledge there are a couple of back-door routes to the Euros in two years' time.

With that in the mind, the new manager will be granted a grace period by punters. Eleven days is more than most are awarded.

title: The issues Mourinho is struggling to fix at Real
description: Jose Mourinho only returned to Real Madrid in July but a lot needs to improve in order for there to be a title race in La Liga.
fullText:
When Jose Mourinho walked back through the doors at Real Madrid this summer, 13 years had passed since he last left the club.

He returned with a familiar reputation and enormous expectations, but facing a very different challenge.

Mourinho was handed a three-year contract, with the club hoping he could restore stability as well as success after two trophyless seasons.

Now, seven league matches into his second spell, some of the familiar tensions of last season have already resurfaced.

Defeat by rivals Atletico Madrid has left supporters questioning Real Madrid's consistency and Mourinho's approach.

The Portuguese coach now has plenty of time to consider his options during an unusually long three-week international break. Madrid do not play again until they host Villarreal on Saturday, 10 October - and travel to Barcelona two weeks later.

Mourinho has concerns about the break, but it is an early opportunity to take stock and prepare for a run of fixtures that could tell us much more about the direction of his second spell at the Bernabeu.

Mourinho prints out 'red card' incidents after Real lose derby

An iron fist joining a broken team: Inside Mourinho's Real return

For Mourinho, the derby defeat at Atletico Madrid was a sobering reminder of the scale of the challenge he has taken on.

Despite blaming much of the loss on two first-half decisions he felt went against his side - Cristian Romero escaping a red card for his studs-up challenge on Jude Bellingham and Lee Kang-in going unpunished for a similar challenge on Federico Valverde - the reality is that their performance was simply not good enough.

It means Real Madrid sit fourth in La Liga, with defending champions Barcelona already six points ahead. They have won all seven of their league games, scoring 31 goals, with Raphinha already scoring 12 times.

Atletico sit second and Real Betis third, both five points behind Hansi Flick's side.

The only time Real Madrid have overturned a six-point deficit to Barcelona at the top of La Liga was in Fabio Capello's 2006-07 title triumph.

A clear issue from the defeat at Atletico was Madrid's lack of control in midfield.

Mourinho started Aurelien Tchouameni alongside Valverde, with Bellingham playing further forward. The pairing gave Madrid energy and defensive security, but they struggled to control the tempo or create enough from deeper areas. Bernardo Silva was introduced for the final eight minutes, but by then Madrid were already chasing the game.

That presents Mourinho with an interesting selection decision. Against opponents who defend in a compact shape, Madrid may need more creativity and control from midfield.

Silva's ability to dictate the rhythm of a game makes him an obvious option, while Arda Guler offers another creative presence further forward.

Mourinho doesn't necessarily need to abandon the double pivot, but he does need to find a way for Real to have more control of matches.

There is no shortage of individual attacking quality at Real Madrid. The problem is making it work consistently as a unit.

Against Atletico, Madrid struggled to create clear chances. Kylian Mbappe was largely ineffective and hardly touched the ball, while Vinicius Jr was substituted shortly after Dean Huijsen's red card early in the second half.

Mourinho has three players, in Vinicius, Mbappe and Bellingham, capable of deciding matches on their own.

Bellingham's ability to carry the ball forward, arrive late in the box and link midfield with attack is another important part of Madrid's attacking threat, but Mourinho needs to ensure the trio complement rather than crowd each other.

Vinicius needs to rediscover the explosiveness and directness that makes him so difficult to defend, while Mbappe needs a greater supply of chances rather than being asked to create opportunities for himself.

There is another attacking option Mourinho could turn to more often.

Carlos Espi has already made an impression since joining the club, scoring the 90th-minute winner against Espanyol on his league debut before doing it again in stoppage time against Elche.

The 21-year-old has therefore shown he can make an impact when given game time.

With Madrid still working out how best to balance Vinicius, Mbappe and Bellingham, Espi offers Mourinho another option - particularly when Madrid need a focal point in the final stages of matches.

His early impact suggests he deserves more opportunities to show what he can do.

The other major concern is what happens when Madrid lose the ball.

Atletico repeatedly found space around Madrid's midfield and were able to attack quickly, while Huijsen's red card made the situation even more difficult. If Mourinho wants his side to press aggressively and commit numbers forward, Tchouameni and Valverde must provide enough protection when possession is lost.

Against Atletico, Denzel Dumfries, Ibrahima Konate, Huijsen and Marc Cucurella lined up in front of Thibaut Courtois. There is quality in that back four, but Mourinho will want greater cohesion - particularly when Madrid's full-backs push forward.

Courtois' performance showed how important he remains, with the goalkeeper making several important saves to keep Madrid in the game. The aim for Mourinho will be to reduce those situations and make Madrid harder to expose when attacks break down.

The veteran Portuguese needs to come up with some new answers to his team's problems quickly, or there may not be much of a title race.

title: The MMA fighter helping Brighton - and filling stadiums
description: From helping Brighton with set pieces to fighting in front of nearly 60,000 people - meet MMA star Christian Eckerlin, who competes at Oktagon 94 in Frankfurt on Saturday.
fullText:
Christian Eckerlin laughs modestly when asked if he feels he has contributed to Brighton's success.

Last season, the 39-year-old MMA fighter was brought in by the Premier League club to help with their training for set-pieces.

Eckerlin was a professional footballer in Germany before transitioning to MMA, and says he taught Brighton players "wrestling, head control, hip control, and how to push back against opponents".

Days before this interview with Eckerlin took place, the Seagulls moved up to third in the Premier League after beating champions and set-piece kings Arsenal 3-0.

Eckerlin is quick to play down the impact of his advice for the Brighton players, but admits his training "opened doors" for them.

"The Premier League is more physical, more aggressive, and they don't know how to use their body," Eckerlin told BBC Sport.

"Brighton sent me videos of how they defend, and they did nothing with their hips and arms.

"I taught them first in the weightlifting room, then the pitch, and it worked. This is what I did, I opened doors for them."

Eckerlin was a professional footballer from 2005 to 2009, playing for SV Darmstadt in the third tier of German football at the peak of his career.

As a youngster, Eckerlin always wanted to play for the team he supports, Eintracht Frankfurt, but believed his dream was over when he left the sport.

Little did he know that MMA, and specifically European promotion Oktagon, would help make his dream of performing there come true.

In 2024, Eckerlin beat fellow German Christian Jungwirth at Frankfurt's Deutsche Bank Park in front of nearly 60,000 fans in the most-attended MMA event of the year.

On Saturday, Eckerlin returns to the stadium also known as the Waldstadion for a second time to face the Czech Republic's David Kozma at Oktagon 94 with nearly 60,000 expected once again.

"It was my first dream, when I was in the Waldstadion when I was six or seven with my uncle. It was the dream for me to play there but I thought the fire went out," says Eckerlin.

"I cannot tell you in words what this means to me. The biggest thing in my career. And now for the second time... crazy.

"I'm at the end of my career, I'm 39, so this is maybe my last fight. There's no better way to stop fighting in my backyard, you know."

'My promise to my late son is what keeps me alive'

Eckerlin grew up in a small town outside Frankfurt called Erbach and says football "was his first passion".

During his youth career he played against stars such as Bastian Schweinsteiger and Mats Hummels, but ended up leaving football at the age of 20 after a disagreement with his coaches.

"I got a little bit crazy and partied with friends. But my popularity went down with the coaches," said Eckerlin.

"They said 'you cannot do this'. But I was young, nobody was on my side to say 'calm down and do your thing'. So I said 'OK, I'm going'."

Eckerlin played at left-back but admits he "wasn't a technical guy" before joking he was more of a fighter on the pitch.

He knows Brighton manager Fabian Hurzeler through a friend who used to play with him in Munich.

It was Hurzeler who invited Eckerlin over to Brighton, where he spent three days with the players.

Eckerlin says all the players did well learning the MMA techniques he taught them, but Danny Welbeck, James Milner and Lewis Dunk "had the feeling for it".

Football remains the most popular sport in Germany, but Eckerlin says he helped grow his following after switching to MMA via his YouTube channel.

He says the fanfare in Frankfurt is "crazy", with fans always wanting to take pictures with him, but adds he is equally as well known in large cities such as Berlin and Hamburg.

With nearly 60,000 fans expected again for his fight on Saturday, the show is likely to be the most well-attended MMA event of the year once again.

Before what Eckerlin describes as probably the final fight of his 26-fight career, he takes a moment to reflect on the impact he's had on MMA in Germany.

"I love this sport, and I push the sport more than everybody or anybody before in this country," says Eckerlin.

"After my career, when I look back, I think then I will realise, what I do for the sport, or for MMA in Germany. But now I'm fully focused, and there's no time to think about the things in the past."

title: Chadwick says driving F1 car 'top of bucket list'
description: Jamie Chadwick says testing a Formula 1 car is the highlight of her motorsport career.
fullText:
One of the world's most decorated female racing drivers, Jamie Chadwick has described testing a Formula 1 car as the highlight of her motorsport career.

Britain's Chadwick joins an exclusive list of women to have driven an F1 car, after taking part in 32 laps at the Portimao circuit in Portugal, which will be on the F1 calendar in 2027.

The 28-year-old first joined Formula 1 team Williams in 2019 as a development driver and has gone on to win all three seasons of the all-female W Series, as well as being the first female driver to win a road race in IndyCar's feeder series.

She told BBC Sport: "In terms of a dream or a bucket list item, it's definitely the top.

"It was pretty surreal. It's kind of everything I imagined, but more. The feeling you get from a car like that is pretty incredible. And then at a track like Portimao, it's a proper rollercoaster."

She practised in a simulator beforehand and took part in a detailed programme of gym work, which included neck strengthening sessions, with some of the drivers on the F1 grid.

"I train my neck anyway for what I do, but it's that times 10. Just the sheer level of strength that's required in the neck is huge," she said.

"I can't really put it into words the G-force and the feeling on your neck. As soon as you accelerate out of the pit-lane, your head hits the back of the headrest because it's so aggressive.

"You wake up the next morning like you've been in a fight with Mike Tyson. It feels like you've been beaten about a bit, but it's an incredible feeling."

There are now 13 women who have driven an F1 car. Five of those have officially entered a F1 Grand Prix weekend, and only two have gone on to actually take part in a race.

Maria Teresa de Filippis made history as the first female in 1958 when she took part in the Belgium Grand Prix, finishing 10th.

It took 15 years to see the next woman in an F1 car. The legendary Lella Lombardi took part in a record 17 grands prix, including the Spanish GP in 1975, where she finished sixth, becoming the first and so far only woman to score points.

In 2014, Susie Wolff made the first female appearance in an official F1 session for more than two decades, when she drove a Williams car at the British Grand Prix.

Wolff, who is now the managing director of the all-female series F1 Academy, has been instrumental in helping more females get into the sport and was one of the "inspirations" behind Chadwick wanting to drive an F1 car.

Chadwick is not the only woman to have driven an F1 car this year. Doriane Pin, who won the F1 Academy title in 2025, became the first female to drive a Mercedes in April.

But despite the progress, no woman has started an F1 race since Lombardi, 50 years ago.

Chadwick believed that women are "capable of competing in Formula 1", but that there "shouldn't be a timeline on it".

"I definitely believe the talent is out there," she said, adding: "And I'm excited.

"Me doing this test and Williams giving opportunities to female drivers for example, will hopefully lead to a race seat one day."

But with only 22 seats in F1, it is extremely tough for any driver to break into.

Chadwick said: "You're looking at F2, F3 champions not getting seats and you realise that there's more talent than there are seats often available. Then you narrow it down to a female driver and it's even tougher and an even smaller talent pool.

"But I genuinely believe with everything that we're doing now to support female talent it's only going to lead in a positive direction."

title: The computer hacker who tried to take down Man City
description: BBC Sport travelled to Portugal to find out more about Rui Pinto - the computer hacker who sparked the Manchester City investigation.
fullText:
Mention Rui Pinto's name to Manchester City fans outside Etihad Stadium, and you mostly get blank faces.

But while they might not know his name, they are more than familiar with his work.

Pinto is the Portuguese computer hacker who tried to bring down City.

Through his website Football Leaks, he published a cache of confidential club documents, including internal emails about sponsorship deals and payments.

That ultimately led to the Premier League charges for breaching of financial rules and Friday's news that the club had been found guilty of the majority of the 115 counts.

For some, 37-year-old Pinto is no more than a criminal who stole information with sinister intentions.

To others, though, he is a bastion of truth who has shone a light on the darker side of the beautiful game.

BBC Sport has been on a journey across Europe to find out more about the mysterious figure who was the catalyst for so much controversy.

We spoke to one of Pinto's former teachers, a Portuguese politician fighting for him to be protected as a whistleblower, journalists who published the leaks, and a former financial adviser at Manchester City.

And we sat just a few feet from Pinto in the latest of his court cases.

With his cherubic face and spiky hair, Pinto is instantly recognisable. And it seems he hasn't changed.

It is how Mario Falcao, his former geography teacher, remembers him.

In a small courtyard garden in Portugal, we got a glimpse of what Pinto was like as a boy.

"Rui was a perfectly normal pupil. He was nice, with his spiky hair, he was quite sociable but not extrovert," Falcao said.

"He had a good relationship with the teachers, although he did miss these classes quite often. His father was always on top of things, so in the end he passed quite easily."

Did he spot a strong interest in computers in a young Pinto?

"Certainly he was very good in computers. All the work that he did for various courses were very good, when he put his mind to it," his former teacher explained.

The now-retired Falcao speaks fondly of Pinto, who he says behaved just like his friends and would "go to the gym, go to McDonald's".

Pinto had a modest upbringing. He grew up in an area called Vila Nova de Gaia, just across the Douro River from Porto, Portugal's second-largest city. We visited the road where he used to live, which featured tile-fronted houses with terracotta roofs.

His school, Escola Secundaria Almeida Garrett, was well-regarded and was known by locals as 'the university'.

His father, Francisco, worked in a shoe factory and later as an antiques dealer. His mother had died when he was 11.

Falcao said he never predicted what was to come of his former pupil.

"We were very surprised," he said of the moment Pinto was named as the founder of Football Leaks in 2019.

"We weren't imagining anything like this could happen, that he could have problems with justice.

"I certainly wouldn't wish him and his family to be in this situation. Perhaps it was a question of the excesses of youth, his ability with computers, and maybe an excess of club-ism."

"So, you know, the fact that he supported FC Porto prompted him to commit some acts, but maybe he also felt the need for justice that young people very often do feel."

Clubs seek legal advice over Man City charges compensation

Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City

Pinto set up Football Leaks in 2015, to - in his words - expose "the hidden side of football".

Antonio Varela remembers the website's launch like it was yesterday. The Portuguese journalist was the first person contacted by Pinto, whose real identity would not be known for years to come, and was initially known by the pseudonym "John".

"It was a common day of September 2015. I was at the news room at [Portuguese sports newspaper] Record and I got an email from Football Leaks. It was strange. Then I immediately go to the site, and I can't believe there is lots of information that you never heard or read. We made the conclusion this is very, very important."

Re-publishing what had been leaked by Pinto brought legal and ethical conundrums.

"We realised that [Football Leaks] got the information illegally. But since the moment they publish the information on the site, that's public information," said Varela.

"You can't ignore that. Ethically, it's complicated, but the public interest is more relevant than the ethical issue. That was the conclusion."

It wasn't just eight-time Premier League champions Manchester City that Pinto targeted.

The early revelations on Football Leaks focused on matters closer to home, with leaks around Benfica and even the side he supported, FC Porto.

Later, there were leaked documents and communications relating to some of the world's most famous players, clubs and agents, including Cristiano Ronaldo, Lionel Messi and Neymar.

Pinto agreed to meet a journalist, Rafael Buschmann from the German magazine Der Spiegel. Once he knew he could trust him, he shared tens of millions of documents with him.

It was then up to a team of journalists in the Der Spiegel headquarters in Hamburg to meticulously go through it all, producing some of the most explosive articles the football world has ever seen.

Christoph Winterbach, a data journalist, was part of that team.

"In the beginning it was very much a fascinating feeling of like a child in a candy store," he said.

"If you're a football fan, if you're a sports journalist, it was amazing to see the actual documents, to see those emails where things are negotiated and to get a real look behind the curtain, how things work.

"It's very important when you have this type of documents, this type of data, that you make a lot of cross checks, that you use some software which we did that can put it all into context and you can see if there's any reliability issues.

"We always need to make sure that it's authentic material and whenever we publish something about it, it needs to be in the public interest to start writing."

Winterbach finally met Pinto in person in 2019, when he was being held in prison in Lisbon awaiting his trial. He conducted another interview with Pinto in witness protection, in a secret location with high security, describing the arrangements for getting there as being "like a Hollywood movie".

He said: "Rui Pinto is not very tall. He has very distinctive hair, like spiky hair. He usually has red cheeks and he's a youthful, cheeky, funny character. He's friendly and warm when you meet him.

"He's a very impressive character, he's very focused, he's very concentrated. He's very, very intelligent. He's very idealistic about the topics that he uncovered.

"He's one of the most important whistleblowers that we have in Europe or maybe the world."

In all, Pinto provided more than three terabytes - equivalent to about 3,000 copies of the Encyclopedia Britannica - of information to Der Spiegel and other outlets in the European Investigative Collaborations consortium.

We encountered stark contrasts in perceptions of Pinto wherever we went.

Former Portuguese politician and diplomat Ana Gomes has also met Pinto in prison and testified on his behalf at one of his trials. She is firmly of the view that he deserves to be protected, not prosecuted.

"What he has exposed is very important. In Portugal, definitely he is by far the most important whistleblower," the former Member of the European Parliament told us in Lisbon.

"He should be made an ally of our judicial and criminal investigative authorities. He has helped the authorities of other European countries in going after the corrupt and the criminals, instead of being the subject of this judicial prosecution by the choice of our public prosecutors."

When asked what she would say to Manchester City, who had their emails hacked by him, her answer is blunt.

"I couldn't care less. If they have nothing to hide, what's their problem?"

Jose Carlos Freitas, a retired journalist, said Gomes's sympathetic view is not a widely held one.

"For the majority of the people, they look at him as a thief," he said. "For some people, he is a kind of hero, a Robin Hood, you can say because he was exposing the dark side of the business of so many clubs, but unfortunately for the majority of the people, he is not a good person."

Varela is on the fence. "Nowadays, I think I put him in the middle [between whistleblower and criminal hacker] because he got the information illegally. But he gave us, all of us, a view, a dark view of European football, so he did a job to the society illegally."

Wherever you sit in the debate, he has faced serious consequences for what he did. As Winterbach puts it, Pinto "has powerful enemies through the work that he has done".

For the past six years, Pinto's life has been far from normal.

Having been arrested in Hungary in 2019, he was extradited to Portugal and has at various points been in solitary confinement, under house arrest and in witness protection.

Following his first trial in Portugal, in 2023 he received a four-year suspended sentence having been found guilty of attempted extortion, illegal access to data and breach of correspondence.

A separate trial in France resulted in a six-month suspended prison sentence a few months later.

And in January last year, Pinto's latest trial began in Lisbon. The opening day at the Central Criminal Court encapsulated the realities of his life and the difference in opinions of him.

Pinto arrived with members of his witness protection team, two of whom stayed in the courtroom throughout the hearing, along with an armed police presence.

He was dressed casually in a blue, long-sleeved top, jeans and brown boots, and had his distinctive spiky hair and some facial hair. He was fairly expressionless throughout, aside from the occasional shrug of the shoulders or glance at his team.

We sat just a few feet from him, as he conversed with his legal team in hushed tones and spoke to the judge purely to confirm details like his name and age. When asked for his address, he said he could not give this for security reasons.

Local journalist Miguel Dantas explained the security arrangements were scaled back compared with the first trial, when he wore a bulletproof jacket and there were snipers on the roof.

Rui Patricio, the lawyer representing Benfica, told the court Pinto was "no more, no less than a burglar", that he had obtained the information by "illegal and condemnable methods" and that the ends did not justify the means.

Outside court, Patricio added: "Our argument is very, very simple. He's a hacker, period, just like that. What he did is not allowed - it's a crime and there are no excuses. It's very, very simple. Very, very straightforward."

In his statement in court, Francisco Texeira da Mota, representing Pinto, accepted that his client was "not a hero and not a saint" but said he had brought "advantages for society".

The impact of Football Leaks is still being felt a decade on.

The Premier League's case against Manchester City has been one of unprecedented scale and significance.

From speaking to his legal team after the court hearing, it became clear Pinto has been closely monitoring that case from witness protection since the Premier League brought the charges in February 2023.

Asked if the outcome mattered, Texeira da Mota said: "I think it's important for him because it's very difficult to be like he is, living a very difficult life, more or less hiding, because he made some revelations, he whistle-blowed lots of important things, namely about Manchester City.

"So it would be important for him to feel vindicated that it was useful, that something happened, because what of what he said."

Speaking before the announcement of the decision in the City case, Stefan Borson, a former financial adviser to Manchester City, said: "I think for City, really, the whole of the Sheikh Mansour era is at stake if the core allegations are proven against the club.

"I think the consequences could be very far reaching for the club, and it would be a very difficult thing for them to deal with.

"Over time, clearly there would have to be some kind of reset. I think in many ways the Premier League is a loser either way."

Borson's view was that Pinto should not be seen as "some kind of warrior for freedom".

He said: "We know that what he carried out was a criminal act and he's been prosecuted for it.

"We also know that hackers of that nature do try and reframe themselves as part of the defence process as purveyors of freedom of speech. But, once those documents are in the public domain, then I think it's for the authorities to act."

For some, Rui Pinto is a criminal hacker who stole information with sinister intentions. To others he is a heroic whistleblower who shone a light on the darker side of the beautiful game.

What is undeniable is that one Portuguese man on his computer in Budapest has had a seismic impact on global football.

title: Do England have a problem against top-10 teams?
description: As England prepare to take on Spain in their opening Nations League match, BBC Sport takes a look at whether they have a problem when faced with teams in the world top 10.
fullText:
When England take on Spain in their opening Nations League match on Saturday, it will be tinged with a feeling of 'what could have been' for Three Lions fans.

The Wembley match comes three months after England agonisingly missed out on the chance to face La Roja in the World Cup final, having lost to Argentina in the last four.

That would have been a repeat of the 2024 Euros final, which England also lost.

In fact, their record against top-10 sides leaves much to be desired.

In their past 15 matches against sides ranked in the top 10 in the world - according to Fifa's rankings - England have won six matches.

Three of those wins were at major tournaments - the Euros semi-finals in 2021 and 2024 against Denmark and the Netherlands, and the bronze-medal match against France at this summer's World Cup.

The victory over Les Bleus to take third place was Thomas Tuchel's first win as England boss over a top-10 opponent.

And his first win over opposition ranked inside the top 20 came in their opening group game at the tournament against Croatia.

So do England have a problem against top-10 opposition?

Six wins in their past 15 games against top-10 opponents are not the kind of numbers an England team with the ambition of winning major tournaments can be happy with.

Two of those wins meant the Three Lions advanced to the Euro finals of 2020 and 2024. One was in the World Cup match no one wants to play in, two were Euro qualifying matches against an Italy side already on a sharp decline and one came against Belgium in a Nations League match six years ago.

To put it simply, when faced with really elite opposition, England continue to stumble. Particularly at the World Cup.

England have been eliminated every time they have faced a top-10 ranked nation in the knockout stages of the World Cup since 1998 - seven times out of seven.

In their past 10 World Cup games against sides ranked in the top 10, their sole win came in the 2002 group stage against Argentina.

When faced with the defending world champions at the World Cup, they have lost on all four occasions.

England have fared better at the Euros, overcoming top-10 opponents in Denmark and the Netherlands to reach the final at the past two tournaments but ultimately falling at the final hurdle on both occasions against Spain (2024) and Italy (2020).

Meanwhile, their lowest possession in their last 15 games against top-10 opponents came in the semi-final against Argentina (35.8%) at this summer's World Cup and in those Euros finals against Spain (34.9%) and Italy (42.1%).

England's all-time top scorer Kane, with 85 goals, was asked which missing ingredient was needed to get them over the line.

"I think it's just in those biggest moments, still being ourselves," he told BBC Radio 5 Live.

"The Argentina game was so hard to take, because we had a mindset of going to win the tournament, win in our way and our style, and if we lose trying to do that then we will take that.

"The Argentina game was maybe the first game we tried 'not to lose' in the last 30 minutes and then we ended up losing anyway."

Kane has scored 152 goals in 154 games for Bayern, winning two Bundesliga titles.

"I have experienced it at Bayern Munich for example, you don't fear anyone," the 33-year-old said.

"You go and be yourself, if a team beats you, shake their hand after and say well done.

"You have an identity that you keep throughout.

"I think with England now that is where we need to look.

"We are very close, we have been very close but ultimately, we don't need to fear anyone.

"We just need to be ourselves in the biggest moments and hopefully get over the line."

England have been getting closer to major tournament glory over a number of years but the same question remains - can they dominate the ball and beat elite opposition?

At Euro 2020, the last-16 win over Germany was huge - beating one of the historic footballing powers. But that was a German side in transition who were, at the time, ranked outside the world's top 10.

England were then beaten by Italy in the final after taking the lead, dropping deep and giving up possession before losing on penalties.

At the 2022 World Cup in Qatar, the Three Lions started the tournament with a free-flowing 6-2 win over Iran. Although this was not top opposition, the change in mentality from previous tournaments was notable.

But yet again the same issues resurfaced. Despite largely being the better team against France, a Harry Kane missed penalty and Les Bleus' know-how put England out at the quarter-final stage.

Euro 2024 proved to be one tournament too far for Gareth Southgate and that team did not play anywhere near their best, relying on individual quality to get them through.

A last-gasp Ollie Watkins strike was needed to beat the Netherlands in the semis while Kane was not at full fitness and without him at his best, the team never troubled a formidable Spain side.

After a flawless 2026 World Cup qualifying campaign and a new elite coach in Tuchel, many thought this was England's time for glory.

But, despite showing a huge amount of togetherness and grit in the last-16 win over Mexico, the same old problems once again sunk England.

The Three Lions cannot seem to translate world class talent into ball possession and control of the game, with Tuchel saying he may have to embrace the chaos, and Anthony Gordon adding that England should lean on their traditional direct style.

Perhaps that is what is needed to finally end their long wait for a trophy.

title: Joshua fight at risk over promoter row, says Fury
description: Tyson Fury says his long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight against Anthony Joshua in December is in jeopardy.
fullText:
Tyson Fury says his long-awaited all-British heavyweight fight against Anthony Joshua in December is in jeopardy because of a row between rival promoters.

The bout was announced earlier this week following years of failed negotiations, with the pair set to fight at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on 11 December.

The event, which will be broadcast on Netflix, was confirmed as a collaboration between Saudi boxing powerbroker Turki Alalshikh's The Ring and UFC president Dana White, but this appears to be the sticking point.

Eddie Hearn, Joshua's promoter, has been at odds with White in recent months, and says the UFC head's involvement is a breach of their contract.

Fury says Matchroom promoter Hearn's reluctance to work with White is putting the fight in doubt.

"Anthony Joshua and Eddie Hearn are trying to pull out of this fight. They're saying they're not going to fight now," Fury posted on Instagram.

"It's mainly to do with Eddie Hearn's ego. He's making up a million different things and threatening we're not going to fight.

"Now you've got Turki Alalshikh finding alternative real men who will fight at the drop of a hand. Eddie Hearn has cost us the biggest fight in boxing history."

Hearn has been publicly feuding with UFC president White since the launch of Zuffa Boxing earlier this year.

Speaking to IFL TV, Hearn said White's involvement in the promotion of the Fury and Joshua fight "ain't happening", despite Netflix's news release.

"Dana White cannot be involved with this fight promotion. Netflix clearly didn't get the memo. No-one talks to each other," said Hearn.

"Then Netflix say the fight is in conjunction with Dana White. Now we have to go through that process and deal with it. It's a little bit annoying but as I've shown through the UK battle that we won, we stand by our contracts."

Fury's promoter Frank Warren said White was influential in securing the deal with Netflix after the fight was confirmed.

Fury's claim the bout could be off follows his post on social media earlier this month suggesting that Joshua, 36, was backing out of the fight, before calling for a third match-up with Oleksandr Usyk.

There was no official statement from Hearn or Warren in the news release sent out by Netflix to announce the fight.

BBC Sport has contacted Matchroom, Warren's company Queensberry Promotions, The Ring and Netflix for comment.

The dispute between Hearn and White is the latest stumbling block following years of failed negotiations around the fight.

In 2020, the two camps agreed the basis of a two-fight deal. In 2021, contracts were signed for an undisputed heavyweight contest, only for Deontay Wilder's successful arbitration case to force Fury into a third fight with the American.

Then, in 2022, Joshua accepted a 60-40 split to challenge Fury, but that attempt also fell apart.

Fury and Joshua finally signed contracts for the bout earlier this year, with the date and venue confirmed this week.

title: TikTok to pay $100M and limit daily child usage in Alabama settlement
description: Alabama was set to take TikTok to trial over claims that it intentionally addicted young users.
fullText:
TikTok and its parent company ByteDance will pay the US state of Alabama $100m (£754.5m) and make a series of changes to restrict children's usage in the state as part of a lawsuit settlement.

The deal was reached just before a jury trial was set to begin on Monday. It ends a lawsuit alleging TikTok is intentionally designed to addict children to its features, mirroring a host of lawsuits against social media platforms.

The company is now required to install a number of new safety features, including a two-hour daily usage limit for children as well as overnight and school-hour restrictions.

The changes will only apply in Alabama. It marks the platform's first settlement with a US state.

"We're very pleased," said Katherine Robertson, chief counsel in the Alabama Attorney General's office in an interview with the BBC.

She added that the state had been engaged in mediation with TikTok in the run-up to trial and that the deal they have now reached was the state's final offer.

"This is very restrictive injunctive relief that's going to require them to change a lot of the policies that we had identified as the culprits in what we call the war on childhood," Robertson said.

The new time limits and usage blocks are due to take effect immediately.

However, TikTok has up to a year to implement other changes included as part of the settlement, such as the establishment of age verification measures.

Many of the measures follow a framework established by an August settlement struck between social media rival Meta and 52 state Attorneys General.

TikTok has agreed to pay up to $300m to Alabama if conditions of the new settlement are not met. The $100m payment is due to the state within 45 days.

Other safety features demanded as part of the deal include a host of measures to allow parents to heavily moderate usage by their children, along with restrictions on some content, and new ways to verify the age of young users.

TikTok will also limit children's accounts being discovered by adults, and notify parents to any "suspicious interactions" between teen users and adult users.

A blanket ban on all cosmetic filters for children will also be put in place.

"TikTok's priority has always been fostering a safe and positive space where people can be creative, discover what they love, and connect with their community," a spokesperson for TikTok USDS said. "This builds on our commitment and core objective to continually enhance our robust safety tools to protect teens."

Earlier this year, TikTok split its business ownership, with a new group of investors taking control of operations in the US. The remainder of the business is operated out of China.

ByteDance, the parent company of TikTok in China, was also part of Friday's settlement as ByteDance remains a minority owner of the US joint venture.
